activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The keys sat in a ceramic bowl by the front door for three days before Victoria touched them. Her father had put them there the morning after her birthday, the small brass L hanging off the ring like a tag on a rescued animal, and every time she passed the bowl she felt the strange weight of being watched by her own future. On Saturday morning she finally lifted the ring out, carried it to the kitchen, and set it on the counter while she ate toast standing up, the way she did when she was nervous and didn't want to admit it.

Dylan arrived at eleven, honking once from the street even though he'd been told not to. He came up the driveway holding his own permit, which he'd gotten two weeks earlier, folded once and softened at the crease like a receipt he'd handled too often. "You're actually going," he said. "I thought you'd postpone again." He had a way of sounding like he was teasing when he was really asking, and Victoria had learned to answer the question underneath.

"One hour," she said. "In the parking lot behind the middle school, then maybe the block." Her father was reading the paper on the porch with the deliberate calm of a man pretending not to supervise, and Dylan waved at him with the folded permit still in his hand.

The car was her mother's old sedan, dour and silver, its bumper held on with a strip of tape that had outlived two winters. Victoria exhumed the driver's manual from under the passenger seat, where it had been living among gum wrappers and a melted crayon, and set it on the dash while she adjusted the mirror. Her reflection looked back at her, eighteen and unmoving, and she thought the mirror was wrong about her, that the person in it seemed far readier than she felt.

The first twenty minutes were a humiliation of small errors. She let the clutch out too fast and the car bucked like a startled horse; she turned the wheel the wrong amount and ended the parking space at an angle no geometry could defend. But then something shifted, the way it does with any new language, when the grammar stops being memorized and starts being spoken. She pulled out of a space smoothly, checked her mirror before reversing, and felt a quiet click of ownership, as though the car had agreed to be hers for a minute.

Dylan, from the passenger seat, was building his own future out loud. He worked out the chronology of the next year like a man planning an empire: permit now, license in the spring, and then, in the summer, the four of them, him driving, windows down, nobody's mother dropping anybody off at anything. "Sofie's cousin said it's like that," he said. "You get the license, you're free."

"That's not how it works, I don't think." Victoria had spent an evening on the licensing website two days earlier, partly to postpone the actual driving and partly because she liked knowing the rules of a thing before entering it. "It's graduated. First the permit, then a provisional license, and it has restrictions before the full one. That's the whole point of it, the stages."

Dylan's face did something complicated. "Restrictions like what?"

"Like you can't just load up the car with your friends the day you pass the test. Not right away." She said it carefully, not cruelly, watching his empire lose a province in real time. He looked out the window at the chain-link fence and the basketball court with no net, and she could see him doing the math on the summer, on Sofie, on the cousin who had apparently lied or been lied to.

"There's no way," Dylan said. "What's the point of even having it then." But his voice had gone flat rather than angry, and she knew that tone, because she had used it herself at fourteen about something she'd wanted too much. She pulled the car to the far end of the lot, parked it between the lines on the third try, and let the engine idle.

On the way home, taking the long block past Ms. Çelik's house because Victoria wanted one more stretch of real road under her hands, Dylan was quiet. Ms. Çelik was in her garden, and she raised her trowel in a small salute as the sedan rolled past at a grandmotherly speed. Victoria realized she was holding both truths at once and couldn't drop either: that Dylan's summer would be smaller than he'd planned, and that the stages existed because people like them, at exactly this confidence, were the reason. She didn't say any of it. She signaled, checked the mirror, and turned onto her own street without stalling once.

Backed into the driveway, engine off, she sat with her hands still on the wheel while Dylan unbuckled. "Next weekend," he said, "you're teaching me the parking lot thing. The smooth way you did it." He was already halfway out the door, already somewhere past his disappointment, or deciding to be.

She watched him go, then looked down at the permit where it sat clipped to the visor, a small paper promise of everything that came after it. From the porch her father folded the newspaper in half and said, "So, same time next week?"

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Mia had forty minutes before the library closed, and she spent the first ten of them watching the same eleven-second clip for the sixth time. It showed a warehouse fire, orange and enormous, with a caption in white letters: THIS IS HAPPENING IN LAKESIDE RIGHT NOW. Marie-Soleil had sent it to the group chat at 4:52 with three exclamation points, and Monica had already forwarded it to her cousin who worked near Lakeside.

Mia's mother worked at the hospital in Lakeside. That was the whole reason she was sitting in the back corner of the public library with her phone propped against a stack of returned magazines, trying to think before she pressed share. Her thumb hovered. She set the phone face down and pulled the keyboard toward her instead, because the library computer had a bigger screen and because Ms. Hu, at the reference desk, had once told her that slow decisions were usually better ones, though she had said it about choosing courses.

Monica arrived at 5:15, out of breath, dropped her bag on the chair beside Mia and leaned in. "My cousin's evacuating. She says everyone's posting it. Are you sending it to your mom?"

"I don't know yet," Mia said. She turned the phone over. "Look at the caption. No news station, no date, nothing."

"So? Someone filmed it on their phone." Monica's voice had gone bellicose, the way it did when she thought someone was stalling. "People are allowed to film fires."

Mia had already screenshot one frame of the clip, the clearest one, the moment when the smoke shaped itself into a kind of hook against the sky. She had read somewhere, in a unit Ms. Hu had assigned on evaluating sources, that you could take an image and search it backward, that there was a site for this. She had not been paying much attention at the time. She typed it in now, half certain she was remembering the name wrong, and the site came up: TinEye, a reverse image search engine. The page looked older than she expected, unglamorous, a plain box asking her to upload a picture. The small print at the bottom said it had been launched in 2008.

"That's the whole problem, isn't it," Monica said, watching over her shoulder. "Anyone can put anything anywhere."

"The opposite, actually." Mia dragged the screenshot into the box. "If it finds where the picture already was, then it wasn't filmed today."

The results took a moment. Then a list appeared, page after page of webpages containing the same hooked smoke, the same orange. Mia scrolled, and near the top of the page she found a sorting option she could change, and she set the results to show the oldest first. The list reordered itself. The earliest entry carried a date from four years ago, a news article about a plastics factory fire two provinces away. Below it, more matches, none of them from this week, none of them from Lakeside at all.

Mia sat back. She felt the particular flatness of being right in a way that helped no one, because the clip was still out there, still gathering forwards, and Monica's cousin was still sitting in traffic on a highway for nothing. On the other hand, her mother was not in danger, and that had been the want driving everything since 4:52. She could not predicate the whole town's panic on one old photo, but she could at least stop being part of its supply.

She typed into the group chat: That fire video is from 2021, factory fire near Redmond, not Lakeside. I checked the image on TinEye, it finds where a picture appeared online before, and you can sort oldest first. The oldest match is four years old. Then she sat with her finger above send, because she knew Marie-Soleil would want to know how she was so sure, and Mia was not entirely sure, only sure enough. The article could be wrong. The date could be wrong. She had checked one thing and it had held, and that was all checking ever got you.

She sent it. Monica was already on her phone to her cousin, saying, "Turn around, it's not even our fire, Monica told me, I mean Mia, Mia checked it." At the reference desk, Ms. Hu was pushing the returns cart past their row, and she slowed, looked at the screen with its list of dated matches, and said nothing, only raised her eyebrows slightly and kept going. Marie-Soleil's reply arrived before closing: wait so should i tell my mom to come home from the shelter? Mia typed yes, then deleted it, then typed it again, and pressed send, and began logging off the computer while the screen behind her still showed the oldest result at the top, four years old, holding its place.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
story:
The desks had been pushed to the walls of Room 114 and replaced with folding tables, and Mr. Mwangi stood at the door checking names against a printed list the way, Benjamin supposed, an actual poll worker would. The senior class election was being run this year with borrowed gravity. Real ballots, real booths improvised from cardboard, a real rule that once your ballot went into the box it could not come back out. Benjamin signed his name, took the stiff card and the golf pencil, and carried them to a booth near the window like a man carrying something that might go off.

He was two weeks from eighteen, close enough that the whole thing felt like a rehearsal for a performance he would soon have to give in earnest. Gabrielle had cornered him outside the cafeteria on Monday and asked, in her flat, unhurried way, whether he was voting, and when he said yes she had held his gaze a moment too long before saying, "Good," and walking on. She was running for class president against Yannick, and Benjamin had known them both since the year the district redrawn its boundaries and threw them into the same seventh-grade homeroom. He had not told either of them which way he was leaning, mostly because he did not know.

In the booth, he read the ballot twice. President of the senior class. Two names, two ovals, one choice permitted. That was where the trouble started, because the trouble had started weeks ago and had only been waiting for a form. Gabrielle had a lugubrious way of talking about the school, its sagging spirit, its wasted talent, as though she were delivering a eulogy for something still alive; it could be exhausting, but Benjamin had watched her spend a whole weekend hauling boxes for the food drive nobody else organized, and the speech was not the substance of her. Yannick, meanwhile, had stood up at the assembly and given a peroration so polished that people applauded at the end of every sentence, and Benjamin had applauded too, and then lay awake that night trying to remember a single thing Yannick had actually promised. Energy, he had promised. Renewal. Nothing you could hold.

The pencil hovered over Gabrielle's oval. Then, because he was honest with himself even when it was inconvenient, he let it drift toward Yannick's. There was a case for Yannick. The student council had been inert for two years under presidents exactly like Gabrielle, decent and grinding, and maybe what it needed was someone who could make people want to be in the room. Benjamin's father, who sold insurance and distrusted eloquence for a living, had said over dinner that you vote for the plumber, not the singer. Mr. Mwangi, who had overheard Benjamin and Yannick arguing about it after class, had said only, "Decide what your vote is for," and refused to elaborate, which Benjamin had found theatrical at the time and now, pencil trembling faintly in the cardboard quiet, found merely accurate.

He began to fill in Gabrielle's oval, and his hand, without permission, kept going, sliding toward the second oval, the way you test ice with a second foot. Two marks. Both candidates. His whole divided self, expressed in graphite. He was perhaps a millimeter into Yannick's oval when he heard himself make a small sound and stopped, heart working, staring at the ballot. He looked toward the tables where the counting would happen. He raised his hand.

Mr. Mwangi came over, and behind him, because she had finished voting early and been appointed a monitor, came Gabrielle. Benjamin kept the ballot turned away, but he had to say something, so he said, quietly, that he had started to mark a second oval. It was Yannick, standing at the door waiting his turn, who called across the room, cheerful and unhelpful, "That's an overvote." Gabrielle crouched beside the booth and said, lower, "If you mark more choices than the contest allows, they don't count it. Not for that race. You'd be voting for nobody."

Benjamin sat with that. Not counted. The machine of the election, indifferent to his sincerity, would take his attempt to honor both friends and convert it into silence. His father's plumbers and singers, Mr. Mwangi's refusal to choose for him, Gabrielle's weekend of boxes, Yannick's bright empty room, they all narrowed to the same point: the ballot did not accept ambivalence, and neither, he understood suddenly, did he. What stayed uncertain was whether he was choosing the person who deserved it or the person he'd known longest, and he could feel that uncertainty sitting in his chest like a coin that wouldn't settle, and he marked over the stray graphite with firm, careful strokes until only one oval held a full dark mark, and folded the card.

He dropped it into the box. Gabrielle straightened up beside him and said nothing, but her eyes went to his hands, then to his face, and stayed there.

"You didn't see which one," Benjamin said.

"I didn't," she said. "But I saw you decide."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
story:
The debate topic was taped to the whiteboard before anyone sat down: should algorithms decide who gets bail? Ms. Whitehead had written it in green marker, and beneath it, smaller, the words "take a side." Marcus slid into his seat by the window, laptop already open, the fans wheezing like something antiquated, and found that Camilo had claimed the front row, which he only did when he intended to win.

"Computers don't get tired," Camilo said when Ms. Whitehead called on him first. "They don't hold grudges. A judge sees a guy's face and his tattoo and makes a call at eleven at night. An algorithm just runs the numbers. It's neutral." He said the word neutral the way people say stainless, like it was a property of the metal itself.

Marcus had taken the opposite side on the sign-up sheet, mostly because Milana had dared him to, and now he sat there with nothing. He believed Camilo was wrong; he had grown up two streets from a courthouse where his uncle had once waited three days for a bail hearing, and something in him bristled at the idea that a spreadsheet could be fairer than a tired human being. But belief wasn't an argument, and Ms. Whitehead graded arguments.

While Camilo kept talking, Marcus typed risk assessment algorithm into the search bar, screening his laptop slightly so it didn't look like he was checking scores. The results extruded themselves down the page, headline after headline, and one kept resurfacing like a log in a river: ProPublica, 2016. He clicked it.

Ms. Whitehead called his name. "Marcus. Rebuttal?"

He looked up. The class looked at him, Camilo most of all, chin propped on his fist, waiting to be impressed. Marcus read the paragraph on his screen twice, fast, then a third time slowly, because the first two times he'd assumed he'd misread it.

"The ProPublica investigation," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he felt. "2016. They looked at a risk tool, COMPAS, the kind judges actually use. They found it misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants."

The room went quiet in a different way than it had been. Milana turned around in her seat. "So it's worse at being wrong about Black people," she said.

"That's what twice the rate means," Marcus said. "Same kind of mistake, double the frequency, depending on who's being scored."

Camilo's hand came up, and Ms. Whitehead let him through. "That's one study," he said. "Maybe the data was bad. Garbage in, garbage out. That's not the algorithm's fault."

"Then it's somebody's fault," Marcus said. "And if you can't tell whose, maybe don't let it decide who goes home before trial." He heard his own certainty and distrusted it a little, because Camilo had a point too: the study was one study, and judges made biased calls every day, and he didn't actually know what the fix was. He held both of those thoughts at once and did not pretend one cancelled the other.

Ms. Whitehead wrote "COMPAS" on the board and underlined it. "For Thursday," she said, "I want each of you to find one more source on this. Not to settle it. To complicate it." She said the last part looking directly at Camilo, and Camilo, to his credit, nodded instead of arguing.

After the bell, Camilo stopped at Marcus's desk on the way out. "That was a good find," he said. "I still think automation helps somewhere. Bail might just be the wrong place."

"Maybe," Marcus said. "Thursday, then."

Milana was waiting in the doorway with her backpack on one shoulder. "So are we starting a club or what?" she said, and held the door open for him.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
On the second Tuesday of July, Tristan smuggled his grandmother's broken bowl into craft shed number two wrapped in his sweatshirt, and Braylon, who was supposed to be glazing ashtrays, noticed immediately. "You've been carrying that bundle around like it's a kidney for transplant," Braylon said, leaning over the picnic table with his brush dripping blue. "What is it?"

Tritan unwrapped it. The bowl had split into three pieces on the day camp started, when he'd knocked it off the shelf at home reaching for his duffel bag, and his grandmother hadn't even scolded him, which was somehow worse. She'd only picked up the shards and said, "It was my mother's," and put them in a drawer. "I'm going to fix it," Tristan said now, arranging the pieces so they almost held together, a circle with lightning in it.

"With glue," said Precious, who had wandered over from the kiln with clay dust in her eyebrows. "Glue and then paint over the crack. That's what my dad did with my lamp. You can barely see the line unless you're looking, and nobody's looking, trust me. Grandmothers have terrible eyesight. It's practically endemic in grandmothers."

Tristan had already thought of that. He'd imagined it on the drive up: the bowl whole again, the crack disguised under a skin of white paint, his grandmother fooled or pretending to be fooled, everyone spared. It was efficient. It got the most happiness for the least trouble, a small private triumph of utilitarianism, as Mr. Ahmed had called it in ethics seminar last spring while the class argued about trolleys. But the idea had begun to incapacitate him with doubt every time he held a shard, because the flaw would still be there, just invisible, and he would always know where it ran.

The camp had one shelf of books nobody touched, left over from some donor's cleaning spree, and that evening Tristan found a thin volume on Japanese ceramics wedged between a waterlogged field guide and a mystery missing its last thirty pages. He sat on the porch of his cabin with a flashlight until the mosquitoes drove him inside, and there it was: a photograph of a black bowl with seams of gold running through it like rivers on a dark map. Kintsugi, the caption read. He read it three times. Repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, it said, so that the break became part of the bowl's history instead of something to hide. He whispered the word out loud to make sure he had it. "Kintsugi."

"It's pronounced how you think," Precious said the next morning, when he showed her the page. She studied the photograph, tilting the book. "So instead of covering the crack, you make it the fanciest part. You underline it. In gold." She looked up. "That is either the smartest thing I've ever heard or the most deranged. Possibly both."

Mr. Ahmed, who ran the craft program and owned, mysteriously, a small locked cabinet of actual art supplies, turned out to have gold mica powder and a bottle of lacquer that had survived three summers. He didn't ask many questions. He unlocked the cabinet, set the materials on the table, and said only, "Take your time. The lacquer takes hours to set, and you only get one clean reposition." Then he went back to arguing with the kiln, which had decided that Tuesday was a good day to die. Tristan worked through lunch. The hardest part was not the mixing, which he botched twice and got right the third time, but the waiting, holding two shards together while the glue of his own impatience failed and he had to start again. Braylon sat across from him the whole time, "supervising," eating a granola bar and offering commentary. "You're sweating on it. Don't sweat on history."

When the last seam dried, Tristan carried the bowl outside into the flat afternoon light. The three gold rivers caught the sun and threw it back warm and orange against the black glaze, and Precious leaned in so close her nose nearly touched the rim. "Okay," she said slowly, like someone conceding a point she'd defended all morning. "Okay, I was wrong. Paint would have been a lie wearing a coat." She turned the bowl a degree at a time, watching the light travel. "Can your grandmother actually eat out of it, though? Or is it more of a shelf situation?"

Tristan hadn't decided yet whether to tell her the truth about how it broke, or whether the gold lines would say it for him. He held the bowl up between his hands, thumbs resting on the longest seam, and felt its whole crooked weight, heavier somehow than before it broke, and better. "Pack it in my sock," he told Braylon, who had already claimed the wrapping duty. "The good socks. The ones without the holes."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: An argument from silence draws a conclusion from what a source fails to mention; historians treat it with caution because writers record only what seems important to them.
story:
Michael had forty minutes before the library closed and a thesis he no longer believed in, which was, he decided, the worst possible combination. His essay draft lay open on the table: the 1968 walkout at Central Tech, he had written, probably never happened, because the town's newspaper, which he had searched all afternoon on the microfilm machine, printed nothing about it. Not a paragraph, not a line. Two hundred students supposedly marched out of a building a mile from the newsroom, and the paper treated it like weather in another country. The silence was total, and he had built his whole argument on it, and now he sat there with a feeling like the floor tilting.

Nada dropped into the chair across from him with her own stack of books, most of which appeared to be about Napoleon. "You look like someone stole your evidence," she said.

"My evidence is fine. I have no evidence. That's the point." He slid the draft toward her and watched her read the sentence he was proudest of, the one about the newspaper's silence being proof. She read it twice, which was already a bad sign.

"Okay, so my grandfather," she said, and Michael groaned, because in his experience no sentence beginning that way led anywhere useful. "No, listen. Last summer I asked him about this riot my aunt swears happened in his village when he was a kid. He has these diaries, he's written in them every day since he was fourteen. I went through the whole year. Nothing. I told him it never happened, the diaries don't mention it. And he laughed." She paused to unwrap a granola bar with the deliberateness of someone about to land a point. "He laughed for a long time. Then he said, 'I wrote down what mattered to me. There were shoes to buy and a girl on the next street. The riot was somebody else's day.'"

"An argument from silence," said a voice behind them, and Fabrice pulled up a third chair without asking, holding a coffee he was clearly not supposed to have in the library. "That's what that's called. My history teacher says historians treat it with caution, because writers only record what seems important to them." He said it with the flat certainty of someone repeating a line that had saved him on a test, then immediately looked wounded when neither of them thanked him.

"So the paper not mentioning it," Michael said slowly, "doesn't mean it didn't happen. It means the editor didn't think it mattered. Or didn't want it to matter." The microfilm machine hummed behind Ms. Sinclair's desk, where she was reshelving with the parsimonious efficiency of a woman who believed each book should travel exactly once. Over the intercom she announced that the study rooms were now available until nine, a reprieve Michael hadn't expected, since the seven o'clock closing he'd been racing had apparently been a rumor started by Fabrice to clear out the loud table.

Fabrice had his own crisis, which he now revealed: he was supposed to be writing about the Congress of Vienna, and he had exactly one source, a textbook that summarized everything in four paragraphs. "It's fine," he said, in the tone of a man negotiating with himself. "Four paragraphs is plenty. Everything's in there." Michael recognized the argument because he had been making a version of it all afternoon: the record is small, therefore the past is small, therefore I can be finished by ten.

He went back to the microfilm. This time he didn't look for the walkout; he looked at what the paper did print that week, and it was astonishing how much of the front page was taken up by a garden club luncheon and an editorial about a proposed parking ordinance, which the city council had apparently moved to abrogate after public complaint. A paper that considered a parking ordinance the news of the week was not a paper that would necessarily notice two hundred teenagers in the street, unless one of them threw something through a window, and even then it might depend on the window. He found a single line, finally, on page eleven, below an advertisement for a hardware store: "Central Tech officials declined to comment on a student disturbance Tuesday." Declined to comment. A disturbance so unimportant it was a paragraph long and buried deeper than the seed prices.

Nada leaned over his shoulder. "So it happened," she said.

"It happened," Michael agreed. "Or something happened. Somebody at the school thought it was worth declining to comment on, which is not nothing." He copied the line onto a notecard, then turned it over and wrote on the back the thing he actually wanted to say: that the sources were partial, that they answered the questions their writers cared about, and that the questions kept changing, which was maybe why historians couldn't stop arguing. He would have to be careful with it. His old thesis had been clean and wrong; his new one was honest and shaped like a shrug. Somewhere between the two, he supposed, was the essay.

Fabrice stood, gathered his one textbook, and paused at the edge of the table. "For the record," he said, "I'm going to find a second source tomorrow. Not because of you people. Because I want a better grade than Nada." He walked off toward the study rooms, and Nada went back to Napoleon, and Michael read page eleven again, running his finger under the line about the disturbance, the whole eleven words the town had been willing to spend on it.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
story:
The community kitchen on Alder Street opened at four on Saturdays, and Zachary was there by ten past, apron already tied, because Ms. Le had promised him the marble slab this week. He was seventeen and had burned through three hobbies since September, but tempering chocolate had held him for a whole month, which felt like a record. The trick, as far as he understood it, was heat and patience: melt the chocolate warm, cool it on the slab while working it with a scraper, bring it back up just enough. Done right, it set shiny and snapped clean when you broke it. Done wrong, it went dull and soft and bent like an eraser, and everyone who ate it was too polite to say so.

Nicola arrived at half past, hair still damp from a shower, carrying the box of strawberries she'd promised to dip. "I still think this is pedantry," she said, watching him spread a puddle of dark chocolate across the marble and gather it back with the scraper. "Chocolate's chocolate. It melts, it hardens, you eat it."

"Snapping is different from bending," Zachary said. "You can hear it. It's like the difference between fresh bread and day-old." He held the scraper out to her. "Feel this. It should be thick but move like syrup."

She touched the ribbon of chocolate on the steel and made a face that meant she was admitting nothing.

They dipped the strawberries together, Nicola's coating streaked and sagging, Zachary's drying with a low satin shine he couldn't stop checking. Ms. Le, who ran the kitchen and asked for nothing except that the sinks be left clean, drifted past with a tray of soup cups for the evening meal and said, "Beautiful work, both of you," in the voice of someone who had decided long ago that encouragement cost nothing and was never wasted. When the last strawberry was set, Zachary slid both trays into the big refrigerator at the back, because the room was warm and he wanted the chocolate firm before the seniors' social hour at six.

At six exactly, they carried the trays out. Nicola got hers first, and Zachary heard her say "huh" in a flat, unhappy tone, and then his own tray came into the light and he saw it: a dry, gritty white coating had crept across the surface of every strawberry, dulling the shine he'd been so proud of, powdering the dark chocolate grey. The room that evening was humid from the soup kettles and the crowd of bodies, and the trays had come straight from the cold.

"It's sugar bloom," said Nicola, and Zachary turned to stare at her, because she was the one who'd called all of this pedantry a week ago. "My aunt makes wedding favours. Moisture condenses on cold chocolate, the moisture dissolves sugar on the surface, and then the sugar recrystallizes as it dries. That's the dusty coating. It's not the chocolate going off." She turned one of his strawberries over, examining it. "It's still edible. It just looks like it's been through something."

Zachary wanted to argue that it wasn't fair, that his tempering had been perfect, and then realized he didn't need to argue at all. "So it's the fridge," he said slowly, working it through. "I put them in the fridge, and the cold made them vulnerable to the warm room." The bloom didn't exonerate his technique exactly, but it cleared the temper itself; the failure had happened after, in the space between the refrigerator door and the table. Somewhere in him, the boy who needed every batch to be flawless and the boy who just wanted to feed people something good settled, briefly, into the same person. He wasn't sure yet which one he'd be next Saturday. He suspected it depended on how the next batch behaved, which felt like an honest way to decide.

From where Ms. Le stood by the kettles, she watched the two of them for a moment before she moved. She had seen a hundred teenagers come through this kitchen, most of them gone within a month, and she had privately classed this chocolate business among the moribund hobbies, another thing to be swept up after. But the boy was looking at his ruined tray with curiosity instead of defeat, and the girl, who had mocked the whole enterprise, was now explaining recrystallization with her hands. She changed her mind about them both in the space of that look, and changed it without ceremony, the way she changed the menu when the delivery van brought surprises.

She took a small bowl from the shelf, ladled soup into it, and set it in front of Zachary. "Eat," she said. "Then next time, cool them on the counter, not in the fridge, and keep the trays away from the steam." Zachary picked up one of the bloomed strawberries anyway, turned it once in the light, and bit it. It snapped.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
story:
The printout lay flat on the kitchen table, weighted at the corners by a mug and two forks, and Levi bent close enough to smell the toner. In the picture a woman sat facing him, straight-backed, a thorn necklace cutting into her throat, a hummingbird hanging dead from the thorns. He had spent forty minutes on the background already, the greens layered over greens, the foliage so dense it flattened the space behind her, and had written one sentence in his notebook: the jungle reads as wall, not world.

The assignment had come from Ms. Kelly on Tuesday, and he remembered it clearly because she had refused to give them the usual biography. "No life story," she had said, slapping the reproduction onto the whiteboard tray. "Colour, composition, symbolism. The painting has to argue for itself." Half the class had groaned. A boy near the window had asked whether they could at least mention the bus accident, and Ms. Kelly had said that if the painting needed the accident, it wasn't doing its job. Levi had liked that, the idea that a picture could be treated like a mathematical proof, everything necessary contained on the canvas.

Now, at home on Thursday night, the proof was going badly. His second paragraph was supposed to handle symbolism, and all he had was a list of animals: a spider monkey at her right shoulder, a black cat at her left, butterflies tucked in her hair, a dragonfly hovering above. He wrote each one down and then sat looking at the column, because a list was not an argument, and Ms. Kelly would circle it in red the way she had circled his last attempt and written "inventory, not analysis" beside it.

His phone buzzed on the table.

Dalia: ok i'm doing the same painting and i need to ask you something before i lose my mind. i counted the animals. monkey, cat, hummingbird, two butterflies, dragonfly. what is each one DOING there

Levi: i don't know yet. the monkey looks calm. the cat is just staring out at you. over her shoulder

Dalia: the cat is the one that's bothering me. my mom says cats in paintings mean the painter hated somebody

Levi typed "that's not a method" and deleted it. He looked again at the black cat, its eyes wide, its head pushed forward past her shoulder so that it met the viewer directly, refusing to stay in the background with the monkey. He opened the library database on his laptop, found the catalogue essay from the show the painting had toured with, and ran a finger down the page. The black cat that peers over Kahlo's shoulder, the essay said, is usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death. He read the sentence twice, then checked a second source, which said the same thing without the hedge.

"Usually," he said out loud, to nobody. The kitchen was empty; his mother was at her shift and would not be back until eleven. He copied the line into his notebook, then crossed out "usually" and wrote it again, because the hedge mattered. If he claimed certainty the cat meant death, he was doing exactly what the boy near the window had tried to do with the bus accident, reaching outside the frame for something to close the argument for him.

Dalia: my mom is going with "she hated somebody" no matter what i say

Levi: don't fight it on her behalf. i found the reading though, in the catalogue essay. the cat's usually read as a symbol of bad luck and death. it stares straight out, so it pulls you into the frame instead of letting you look past her

Dalia: oh. that's so much better than "she hated somebody." can i use the staring part

He said she could. He was aware, typing it, that the staring part was his, and that giving it away cost him nothing, because the sentence he was building was going to be different anyway. His mother had a way of describing his uncle's old letters as florid, and he could see now what she meant: an argument that ran every sentence through the same ornament, no variation in weight. He would not write that. The subtlety he wanted was in the contrast itself, the dead hummingbird hanging beside the living cat, the soft monkey beside the flat stare, and the way her face permitted none of it, gave nothing away, held the composition together by refusing to react to her own symbols. Whether she had chosen the cat for death or for balance, or for some third thing no essay had named, was where his proof ran out, and he decided he would say so in the last line rather than pretend otherwise.

He was still drafting when another message arrived, from Marilou this time: i know you're ahead of me. swap partners? dalia already has you. i want someone who's actually done the reading, not someone who shows up with nothing and takes my notes. He looked at the two messages stacked on his screen, Dalia's question and Marilou's want, and typed back that he'd ask Ms. Kelly tomorrow, then set the phone face-down beside the forks and picked up his pen.

"On Friday," Ms. Kelly had said at the end of Tuesday's class, "you defend it out loud." Levi drew a small cat in the margin, gave it the same flat stare, and started his third paragraph: "The animals do not agree with each other."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The envelope was thin, which everyone knew meant no, except that Jackson's answer was not an envelope at all but a portal login that refreshed to the same gray screen no matter how many times he pressed the button, like a door that pretended to be impermeable but was really just slow. He refreshed it in Mr. Oyelaran's fourth period economics class, under the desk, which was its own kind of economics: risk of confiscation versus probability of news. The probability of news was zero, because decisions came out Friday at five, and it was Tuesday, third period lunch having proved that rumors otherwise travel faster than the bell.

"You're doing the face," Quentin said, leaning across the aisle without permission, as was the armistice they had negotiated years ago and never bothered to write down. "The refresh face. Your thumb has a soul now, Jackson, and it's sad."

"It's called diligence," Jackson said, and turned the phone face-down like a card he was bluffing with.

Mr. Oyelaran, who had the unnerving habit of hearing whispered conversations from the far side of the room the way a whale hears the ocean, said, "Since Mr. Jackson is so energetic, perhaps he can tell us why a store offering discounts in December might not actually be losing money." Jackson said something about volume, and Mr. Oyelaran said, "Closer," in the tone of a man awarding half a point, and moved on, and the class resumed its low oceanic murmur about supply curves.

It was Billy, at lunch, staring into a burrito as if it owed him money, who accidentally started the whole thing. Billy had gone on a campus tour the week before with his older sister, and he reported, with the flat wonder of someone repeating a foreign phrase, that the tour guide had stood in front of the library and said the college was proud of its yield, and when a senior on the tour asked what that meant, the guide had said, "Yield is the percentage of students we admit who accept the offer and enroll." Billy had written it on his hand because his sister made him. He showed them the smudged ink as evidence, like a man presenting a fish he had caught.

"Percentage of admits who say yes," Quentin said, chewing. "That's it? Why brag about that?"

Jackson was quiet for the rest of lunch in a way that his friends noticed and honored by talking about a video game instead. In fifth period study hall he drew it out in the margin of his Spanish homework. A college admits a hundred students. Some number say yes. That number, over a hundred, was the yield. Which meant that when he had opened his own admissions portal back in November and pressed the button marked early decision, he had not merely been saying I want to go there. He had been a data point, a sure thing, one guaranteed numerator in their percentage. His desire was, from the other side of the desk, a number they could count on before he even had the answer. He found this both insulting and weirdly flattering, the way you might feel discovering you had been quoted in a paper you never gave an interview to.

By Friday, fifth period, the gray screen still said nothing, and the school day had achieved a texture of pure taffy. Mr. Oyelaran, perhaps out of mercy or perhaps because he was also a person with a portal somewhere in his life, let the last ten minutes dissolve into free time, which in that classroom meant arguing about whether the vending machine's pretzels constituted a monopoly. Jackson raised his hand anyway, for no reason he could have defended, and asked, "If a business knows certain customers will definitely buy, does it treat them differently?"

Mr. Oyelaran considered him over his glasses. "Does the business exist to aggrandize itself, or to serve customers? Perhaps both, perhaps neither. What do you think?"

"I think both," Jackson said. "I think it can want your money and also actually want you." He heard how it sounded a second too late, and Quentin made a small angelic face of delight, and Billy said, "He said want you," and Jackson threw a pencil at him, which Billy caught, because Billy had always been annoyingly athletic in pointless ways.

At 5:04, sitting on the curb outside the school because home felt too far and the curb felt like a place where a person could have a destiny, Jackson pressed refresh. The screen did its gray hesitation, then the gray cleared, and there was a border around something, a color, a word beginning with C, and he was aware simultaneously of Quentin and Billy materializing on either side of him, one reading over his shoulder and one saying don't tell me don't tell me, and of his own heart going about its business without asking him.

"Read it out," Quentin said.

Jackson read it out.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Brooke had spread a sheet of plywood across two lawn chairs in the backyard and was gluing pencil shavings into a spiral, each curl sorted by shade, graphite-dark at the center fading to pale cedar at the rim. The shavings had taken two weeks to collect. She had sharpened down eleven pencils from the mug by the phone, and the porch smelled like wood shavings and the sunscreen still on her arms.

Her little cousin sat cross-legged on the grass with a pencil in his mouth, gnawing the yellow paint off in flakes. He was nine and had been sent over for the afternoon while his mother ran errands, and he had appointed himself her assistant, which meant handing her shavings she could already reach.

"Spit it out," Brooke said, but not urgently. "Why are you even chewing that?"

He spat the flakes into his palm and looked at them, then at her, and his voice dropped like he was confessing something. "At school Conner said a kid died from chewing pencils. Lead poisoning. There's lead inside them. Lead is poison."

Brooke turned a shaving over in her fingers and considered the boy's small worried face. He genuinely thought he had been poisoning himself in installments all morning, the way you might desensitize yourself to a bad idea by repeating it, except he was doing the opposite, sensitizing himself to a fear. "There's no lead in it," she said. "People just call the black stuff lead, but it's actually graphite. It got the name back in the 1500s because when they first found graphite, they thought it was some kind of lead ore." She said it plainly, the way she'd explain anything to him, and watched the worry shift sideways on his face, not quite gone, looking for somewhere else to land.

"So I'm not going to die?"

"You're not going to die from a pencil." She handed him a stub. "Here. Chew this one, it's already ruined."

He chewed, mollified, and Brooke went back to the spiral, and it was while she was pressing a dark shaving into the wood that she heard the gate latch. Ria came through it holding her phone out at arm's length, the way she did when she was carrying evidence. Ria had been her best friend since seventh grade, and for the last three weeks they had been quietly not talking about the district art show, where they were both entered. Quietly, but constantly. The not-talking had become its own conversation.

"Sarah sent me this," Ria said. She set the phone on the plywood, screen up, next to the spiral. On the screen was a photo from the show's website, an entry titled Pencil Spiral, submitted by Ria Delgado, except the thumbnail image was Brooke's spiral. Somebody at the school office had swapped the files when they uploaded the entries.

Brooke looked at her own work wearing her friend's name and felt something she couldn't immediately file. "That's mine," she said, which was obvious, which was the whole problem, and also not the whole problem.

"I know it's yours." Ria took the phone back but didn't put it away. "I emailed them. They said they'll fix it by Friday." She stood there with the phone held against her stomach, and the subtext arrived before the text did, the way it does with people you know well. "Brooke. Did you see the other entry? Mine?"

Brooke had seen it. Ria's piece was a plaster hand, wrist down, the fingers tipped with pencil points, called Graphite Touch, and Brooke had thought it was better than her spiral, honestly better, and had told almost no one that, and had felt the thought sit in her like a stone she was ashamed of. "Yeah," she said. "I saw it."

"And?" Ria's chin was up, her arms crossed now, braced for the bombastic version, the rival version, the version the art show had accidentally cast them in. Brooke recognized the pose because she had worn it herself in the bathroom mirror that morning.

"And it's better than mine," Brooke said. "I've thought that since Tuesday. I was going to say something and then the file got switched and suddenly it looked like I didn't have to say anything, like the universe had made me the winner for free, and I just let it sit there for a day." She pressed another shaving down, needing her hands busy. "Which I guess makes me an egoist, or close to one. I don't actually know what the line is between keeping a good thought to yourself and being a person who would take credit they didn't earn. I don't think I crossed it. But I don't know exactly where it is either."

Ria sat down slowly on the grass beside the cousin, who was watching them both with a pencil in his teeth like a man smoking while a building burns. "Friday," she said finally. "They fix it Friday."

"Friday," Brooke agreed. She picked up the darkest shaving she had left, the one from the center-most pencil, and held it out to Ria over the half-finished spiral. "You want to put one in?"

Ria took it and pressed it into the wood at the edge of the dark center, where it belonged, and the cousin said, around the pencil, "So it's really not lead at all?"

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
The playground behind the elementary school had one bench still upright, and Payton claimed it with her notebook while Anne-Marie paced the wood chips like a lawyer about to close. Michaela sat cross-legged on top of the slide platform, reading off her phone. "Okay, question four. Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer." She looked up. "You've never had a customer. You've never had a job."

"I've had teachers," Payton said. "Teachers are customers who grade you."

"That's not an answer, that's a joke, and jokes are what people do when they're scared." Anne-Marie stopped pacing. "You're doing the thing. With your eyes. You looked at the swing set for that whole sentence."

Payton made herself hold the look, which was worse, because now Anne-Marie's face was doing something careful and pitying. She had an interview Thursday at the garden center, four o'clock, and her mother had already texted twice from her night shift, once to say good luck and once to ask whether Payton had figured out what to do about the part where they ask about experience. She had not. She had a notebook with eleven questions copied from the internet and a page of answers that all began with "I would" and then trailed off into margin doodles.

Michaela came down the slide without using it, just walking, and held the phone out. "It says here they're behavioral questions. Tell me about a time when, that kind. It says they're built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior." She scrolled. "So you're not supposed to say what you would do. You're supposed to say what you already did."

"Then I'm dead," Payton said, "because what I already did was nothing."

"You did the plant thing," Anne-Marie said. "For Mr. Mensah, junior year. The courtyard thing." She turned and pointed at the row of window boxes visible over the school's back fence, the ones Payton had organized when the environmental club collapsed and left forty seedlings in a storeroom. She had built a watering schedule, bullied two sophomores into signing it, carried milk jugs from the gym fountain for three weeks. The plants had lived. It had felt, at the time, like a small unglamorous chore, not at all like a qualification.

"It's not a customer," Payton said, but she was already writing, because a difficulty is a difficulty, and the dead seedlings had been dying, and she had made a schedule and kept it. "Difficult customer: forty tomato plants with no water. Action: I made a schedule." Saying it aloud on a playground made it sound absurd and also, she admitted, like something a person had actually done, which was more than her page of woulds had ever managed. The evening softened. A man she didn't know wheeled a stroller across the far end of the blacktop, and the chain of the baby swing ticked in the wind with a slow, lugubrious patience, and for a while the three of them traded stories back and forth, mining two and a half years of high school for evidence of themselves. Michaela told one about talking a cashier into refunding a cracked phone case, and Anne-Marie told one about a group project, and Payton noticed that the true ones were always less flattering and somehow more convincing. She crossed out half her notebook.

On Thursday she sat across a foldout table from a woman with a lanyard, and the first question was about availability, and the second was about weekends, and the third was whether she could lift thirty pounds of soil. Payton kept her eyes steady anyway, because she had practiced that, and it was almost funny, the effort of holding a gaze that kept dropping to the application form. Then, at the end, when Payton had begun to gather her bag, the woman looked up properly for the first time. "One more. Tell me about a time you had to keep something going when nobody was making you."

It was so close to the question she'd feared that her prepared answer surfaced whole, the dying tomatoes, the milk jugs, the schedule taped inside the storeroom door, and she told it plainly, without the cushion of a joke, watching the woman's face the whole time. She was honest at the end of it, because it seemed wrong not to be: "That was a school thing, not a job. I know it's not the same." She could not tell whether the admission helped or hurt, and she carried that not-knowing out through the greenhouse aisles and all the way home, where it sat beside her at dinner.

The message came Friday while she was at the playground again, this time alone, redoing the wood chips under the bench because someone had scattered them and it bothered her, which she recognized, mid-motion, as exactly the genus of behavior the interview questions were built on. The text was two lines. She had gotten the job, Saturday mornings and two afternoons, starting next week. She read it twice, and the second time she noticed the line underneath, the one the woman had added before her name: that the tomato story had been what did it, that it was the only reason she'd made the cut, since honestly, the availability answer had been a mess.

Payton put the phone face-down on the bench and picked up another handful of wood chips, smoothing the pile flat where the wind had opened it.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In his 1865 book The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption.
story:
The notice board outside the cafeteria said that Ridgemont's bulb drive had been a triumph, and Sophia had taped the town's utility numbers beneath it in blue marker, which spoiled the triumph a little. Total electricity use in the quarter after the drive was up, not down, even though four hundred households had swapped their old bulbs for efficient ones. She had expected applause at the Environmental Club meeting and instead got a silence long enough that she counted the ceiling tiles above the whiteboard.

"Maybe people are just leaving them on more," Ayla said. "They cost less to run, so nobody bothers switching them off." Ayla's father managed the hardware store that had supplied the bulbs at a discount, and Sophia noticed how carefully she said it, the way she always softened anything that touched her family's business. "That's not a reason to regret the drive."

Patrick, who had a mannerism of clicking his pen when a problem interested him, clicked his pen three times and then held it still. "So efficiency backfired. We should tell everyone to go back to candles." He grinned at his own joke and nobody else did, which he seemed to take as confirmation of his comedic genius.

Sophia said she would look into it before the next meeting, and that afternoon she did what Ms. Aziz had taught her to do with any puzzle: historicize it. Find out whether it had happened before, to someone else, in another century, and see what the people of that time made of it. Ms. Aziz, consulted in the library's history section, said only, "Victorians. Try the shelf under the window, the one with the dusty spines," and went back to her cataloguing, which Sophia took as a kind of map.

The book was The Coal Question, from 1865, and the author was William Stanley Jevons, and by the time the library closed she had the passage copied into her notebook in her small square handwriting. Jevons had observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption. She read it twice on the bus home, because it seemed to be saying something impossible. Better engines, more coal. Better bulbs, more electricity. She thought about Ayla's father pricing the bulbs so low that buying them felt like an act of conscience, altruistic and thrifty at once, and about the flyers that had promised savings, and about her own mother running the new kitchen light all evening because it barely cost anything now.

At the next meeting she put her notebook page on the document camera, which was Patrick's idea, and let the whole fact sit on the screen in silence. "It happened before," she said. "Steam engines, coal, the whole country." She admitted what she still didn't know: whether the town's numbers were really the same thing, whether the rise came from lights at all, whether growth in the spring had swallowed the savings, whether anything they had done mattered in the way the flyers had promised. She had a considered position and it had holes in it, and she said so out loud, which felt like standing on a diving board.

Ayla argued that cheaper light was still good, that people with less money could now afford brightness, that Jevons or no Jevons, savings for a household on a tight budget were not nothing. Patrick argued that if you wanted total use to fall you had to make the price tell the truth, and someone had to be brave enough to say so at the town meeting. They went around twice, and Sophia took notes on both sides and could not pick one, and said that too.

Then the vote came, on whether to run a second drive in the autumn, and it passed unanimously, largely because the club had already ordered the flyers and the principal had promised an announcement over the PA. Patrick clicked his pen and said, "So we're doing the thing that raised the numbers." "We're doing the thing that helps people afford light," Ayla said, and Sophia, who genuinely believed both sentences, moved for the minutes to record that the club's position was complicated.

Afterward she stayed to take down the utility numbers from the notice board, out of some instinct about honesty, and behind her she heard two freshmen reading the blue marker. "Use is up," one said. "Because of the bulbs?" The other shrugged. "So we should get more of them, then. It's the one thing our house can actually do." Sophia folded the paper in half and put it in her bag, and didn't say anything at all.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The interview at Hartley's Hardware lasted eleven minutes, which Megan chose to read as efficiency rather than indifference, since the alternative reading did not augur well for her Saturday afternoons. The manager, a woman named Ms. Mercado who kept a jar of wing nuts on her desk the way other people kept candy, asked four questions, looked at Megan's one-page résumé twice, and said, "You start Saturday. Bring a pen."

Megan had wanted the job for reasons she could list: her own money, a bike that wasn't her mother's, the principle of the thing. Lara, who had a theory about everything, claimed that anyone who wanted to work at sixteen was secretly a hedonist in training, saving up for pleasure with the discipline of a monk. Lucius disagreed, on the grounds that Megan didn't actually want anything specific yet, which he said was worse. Megan thought they were both flattering her. She mostly wanted to know what it felt like to have a paycheck, the way you want to know a language by living inside it rather than by studying the grammar.

Saturday morning, Ms. Mercado slid a clipboard across the counter. "Paperwork first. Then I'll show you where the bolts live." The form on top had a number in the corner and the words Employee's Withholding Certificate. Megan read the first line, which asked her to claim dependents, and then the second line, which asked about other income, and felt the form receding from her the way a pool floor does when you can't touch the bottom. She was sixteen. She had never had income of any kind, other or otherwise.

She took out her phone and texted her mother: what do I put on this thing. Her mother was at work and answered in fragments over the next ten minutes while Ms. Mercado rang up a man buying sandpaper. It's called a W-4, her mother wrote. Your boss uses it to know how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. Megan stared at that. Withhold. She had assumed taxes were something that happened later, in April, like a dentist appointment you scheduled when you were an adult. Apparently a piece of it came out of every check, before the money was even hers, and the form was how the store knew how much to take.

"So I just put zero everywhere?" she asked Ms. Mercado, pen hovering.

"Zero or one, depending. Your mom walking you through it?" Ms. Mercado didn't sound like she thought this was babyish, which Megan noted and appreciated. Ms. Mercado, it turned out, was sanguine about nearly everything, including the shoplifter last month and the time the ceiling leaked onto the plumbing aisle. "People stress over that form. It's the wrong thing to stress over. The bolts are alphabetized by feel, not by size. That's the thing to stress over."

Megan filled it out slowly, printing where it said print, and when she finished she read it over once, the way she'd been taught to reread proofs in geometry. It occurred to her that she had never before signed a document that meant anything. The signature looked exactly like her ordinary one and completely different at the same time, like hearing your own voice on a recording. She wondered whether it was possible to feel the exact moment a form became a fact about your life, or whether it only became one later, retroactively, on payday.

Her mother texted again while Ms. Mercado was showing her the bolt wall: it's not a scam, it's the same form I do every year, you get it back or you don't depending. Megan pocketed the phone without answering, because there was a customer, a woman with a paint chip in her fist, asking where the primer was, and Megan actually knew, having been shown the primer aisle four minutes earlier. She walked the woman over, and the woman said "thanks, sweetheart," and Megan decided not to mind that, this once.

Behind the register, waiting for the next customer, she thought about Lara's theory and Lucius's counter-theory and the small line of tax that would be missing from her first check, and she could not yet say which of them the missing line proved right. Maybe none of them. Maybe she'd know in April. The bell over the door jingled and Ms. Mercado called out, without looking up, "Megan, aisle six. Somebody needs a hinge."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
story:
The binder lay open on the tailgate of the pickup, weighted at one corner with a stone because the wind off the hay field had opinions. Jack had been at the diagram for forty minutes: a cell drawn large, the mitochondria sketched in as a kidney shape with folds inside it, like something that had been folded and refolded by a careful hand. The exam was Monday. Monday was two days away, and he was still unsure where to put the first arrow.

Morgan came around the corner of the barn carrying two eggs, which was a strange thing to carry in one hand, and stranger still because the hens were supposed to be shut in. "Keely's coming," Morgan said. "She texted me from the curve in the road." Morgan's family owned this farm and Morgan wanted, more than anything Jack had ever watched a person want something, to take it over after graduation and make it pay, which the farm had not done in some years. Everything Morgan did was angled toward that. Even the eggs were part of it: a trial flock, a spreadsheet, a plan to sell at the Saturday market.

Keely arrived on her bike with her textbook strapped to the rack, hair flat with sweat, and dropped onto the grass beside the tailgate. She leaned over Jack's diagram and frowned at it. "You've got glucose going into the mitochondria," she said. "First arrow. Straight in."

"Where else would it go? That's where the ATP gets made. Ms. Siddiqui said the mitochondria is like the power plant."

"The power plant," Morgan said, delighted, "is not where the coal comes from the ground."

"It's a diagram, not a coal mine," Jack said, and heard his own voice go belligerent, which surprised him, because he was not a belligerent person. He put his pencil down. The wind lifted the corner of the page and the stone did its work.

In September, before any of this, Ms. Siddiqui had kept him after class in the lab that smelled faintly of the ethanol they used to wipe the counters, and had said, "You draw like someone who wants the answer to look tidy. The cell is not tidy." He had thought she was being unfair then. He thought now that she had been giving him something, the way she gave out pens from a coffee mug on her desk without ever asking for them back. He could still see her tapping the diagram on the smartboard with the fat end of a marker, refusing to say more.

He opened the textbook to the chapter he had read twice and half-read a third time, and Keely, without being asked, started flipping from the front, because she read indexes the way other people read gossip. It was Morgan, though, who found it, egg still in one hand, finger jammed against a paragraph while the egg balanced dangerously over the page. "There. Glycolysis. It happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria."

"Read it again," Jack said.

"Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP." Morgan read it slowly, tasting the sentence, and Jack felt the strange enrapture of a fact rearranging a picture he had already drawn, the pencil lines on the tailgate going soft in his mind and redrawing themselves.

So the first arrow did not touch the kidney shape at all. Glucose sat in the cytoplasm, the ordinary jelly of the cell, the part he had shaded in as background, and got split there, into two pyruvate molecules, and the splitting paid out two ATP, net, before anything reached the mitochondria. He drew it. The arrow began in the middle of nowhere, in the part of the cell he had treated like the margin of a page, and only then did the pyruvate travel inward, through the folded wall, into the place where the rest of the story happened. Two ATP. He wrote it small, beside the splitting. He had wanted everything to begin at the destination, and instead it began in the open field, so to speak, before the gates.

"Jack," Keely said, "my dad does that. Shows up at the job site and starts carrying lumber before anyone's even unrolled the plans." She was quiet a second. "He calls it leading from the front. Mostly it just means he does the first part wrong and fast."

"That's pedantry," Morgan said, pointing at Jack's tiny two ATP, the word deployed with total confidence and total wrongness.

"It's a number," Jack said. "Pedantry is when you correct somebody about nothing." He looked at what he had drawn, at the cytoplasm doing work he had assigned to the organelle, and he found he liked it better this way, though he could not fully say why, and he was not going to pretend he could. Maybe the cell, like a farm, did its first work wherever there was room. Maybe that was a reach. He left both possibilities standing and did not write either one down.

Morgan's phone buzzed: the grain co-op, calling back about the egg order, and Morgan went off toward the house at a trot, jacket flapping, saying over one shoulder, "Sunday, the diagram has to be done Sunday, we still have the whole second half." Keely stayed on the grass, turning the textbook toward the light, reading the next section to herself with her lips moving. Jack picked the stone off the page, folded the diagram in half along the line where the cytoplasm ended and the mitochondria began, and put it in his back pocket, where it made a stiff square against the denim all the way to the fence and back.

"Six dozen," Morgan said, returning, holding the phone out flat like an offering. "Six dozen a week, if the hens keep laying. Put that in your diagram, why don't you."

"Cells don't lay eggs," Keely said.

"Then put in the six," Jack said, and opened his binder again.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
Simon had commandeer the family computer an hour ago, when his mother was still pretending she might need it for her banking, and now the kitchen smelled like her coffee and the screen glowed with nine open tabs, each one an apartment he could not quite afford. The deadline was Friday. The building on Rosedale wanted first and last month's rent together, twelve hundred and twelve hundred, plus a damage deposit of six hundred, which meant that before he could sleep in a place, he had to hand over three thousand dollars for the privilege of being poor in it. He was eighteen, he had been accepted to the college downtown, and his savings, earned over three summers at the garden centre, came to two thousand four hundred dollars.

Lewis had texted him a photo of his own solution, a basement suite with a ceiling so low that in the photo his head appeared to have been cropped off. "Beggers cant be choosers," Lewis had written, misspelling it, and then, "also i think beggars." Victor, meanwhile, had a theory. Victor always had a theory. He had come over with energy drinks and commandeered the second chair, spinning it, and now he was delivering the theory: that renting was throwing money away, that everyone should buy, that his uncle had said so.

"That's specious," Simon said, not looking up. He had learned the word in English and had been waiting weeks to use it. "You're eighteen. You'd need a down payment, like tens of thousands, and the bank has to lend you the rest. You don't have tens of thousands. You have a PlayStation."

" concept," Victor said, wounded. "I'm talking concept."

The concept, as far as Simon could assemble it from the tabs on the screen, worked like this. A mortgage was money the bank gave you to buy a place, and you paid it back over decades, and on top of the mortgage you needed a down payment up front, a chunk of cash that proved you were serious. Meanwhile renting required no down payment but did require the deposit, which supposedly came back to you someday, assuming you did not burn the place down. His biology flashcards were stacked beside the keyboard from the night before, antigen on top, the molecule that triggers the immune response, and he kept reading it sideways as home equity, as though one definition might infect the other.

His grandmother called at four, which she did most Sundays, and Simon answered because his mother was out. She was selling her house. She said it in the flat way she announced weather. She was moving to the apartment near the hospital, the one with the garden, and she was selling to a young family who had looked at it twice.

"Mrs. Okafor across the street is selling too," his grandmother said. "She'll get a decent price. But I'll come away with far more, because my house has been paid off for years. Hers hasn't." Simon, holding the phone with his shoulder, opened a new tab.

"Far more how?"

"Home equity," she said. "The home's value minus what's still owed on the mortgage. My owed is nothing."

He typed it. He read it twice. He sat with it while his grandmother described the garden apartment's balcony, and he understood, slowly, the way he understood things best, that the woman across the street could sell her house for the same money and walk away with much less of it, because a share of her sale had a prior engagement with the bank. Ownership was not a single thing. It was a slice, and the slice grew as the owing shrank, and his grandmother's slice was the whole pie.

"So the family buying your house," he said, "they'll own like, one slice of it at first."

"Ninety percent of one slice, if they're sensible," she said. "The rest is the bank's until they've paid. Now tell me about your apartment."

He told her about the three thousand dollars and the two thousand four hundred in his account, and how his mother had offered to cover the gap and he had said he'd think about it, and how Friday was the deadline. Victor, still spinning in the chair, mouthed down payment? and Simon waved him off.

"They're not opposite things, renting and buying," Simon said to his grandmother, or partly to himself, or possibly to Victor. "They're the same problem at different sizes. Cash up front, then the long part." Though even as he said it he wasn't sure that was true. He was sure about the numbers on the screen. He was sure about equity now, in the way he was sure about antigens, definitionally, without knowing what it felt like from inside. Whether renting this apartment at nineteen hundred a month was a reasonable slice of his life to sign away, or whether it was exactly the kind of thing his mother would call a decision made at a spinning desk chair, he genuinely did not know, and he found he could hold both possibilities at once without falling between them.

He asked his grandmother if he could call back Sunday, and she said of course, and mentioned the balcony again.

Victor had stopped spinning. "So what's the move?"

Simon looked at the tab with the Rosedale unit, the little balcony in the photo, twelve hundred a month. He picked up his phone and texted Lewis: "asking about the basement suite. does the ceiling have a middle." Then he opened a calculator, and typed two thousand four hundred minus the deposit, and stared at the number that was left.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
I did not care about the juried show, and I want that on record before anything else. The flyer had been taped to the door of the art room since September, curling at one corner like something vestigial, a leftover from a school year that had not yet earned it, and I had walked past it maybe forty times without reading the whole paragraph. What I cared about was the pencil drawing I'd been building for three weeks: the stairwell behind the gym, rendered in so many layers of graphite that the paper had started to shine.

The problem arrived on a Tuesday. Madelaine was working two tables over, copying a photograph of her brother's dog onto cheap sketch paper, and she kept dragging the side of her hand across what she'd finished. Within ten minutes the dog's muzzle had gone grey and formless, like the animal was dissolving into fog. She held the sheet up to the window and said a word she'd borrowed from her mother.

"Which pencil did you use?" Rafael asked her. He was supposed to be glazing a bowl, but the wheel had claimed his attention the way a fire does.

"This one." She held up the stub, its end black and greasy.

"That's the soft one," I said, before I remembered I'd decided not to talk to her that week. I turned the pencil and read the letter stamped near the eraser. "A 6B. The core is graphite mixed with clay. More clay makes a harder pencil, lighter marks, and those are the H ones. Less clay means softer and darker, and they get the B. Your 6B is mostly graphite. That's why it smears when you touch it."

She looked at me, then at the pencil, then at me again. "So what do I do?"

"Start over on the good paper. Use an H for the light fur, an HB in the middle, and only a 2B where it's actually black. Don't blend with your hand. Blend with this." I gave her my paper stump, which was itself nearly worn to nothing, and she took it without saying thank you, which I decided was fine between us.

I want to be accurate about why we weren't speaking, though my version of it has been challenged. My version: she had told Rafael that my stairwell drawing was "trying too hard," and Rafael, who repeats things the way a bell repeats being struck, had passed it along in the parking lot. Her version, which I found folded into my supply drawer on Wednesday, read as follows: "Jason, I never said your drawing was trying too hard. I said the show was trying too hard, the whole idea of a juried show at a high school, and you weren't even in the conversation. You left before I finished the sentence. I know you think you heard what you heard. Come look at the dog. M." I read it twice. It's possible I left before the sentence ended.
