It's also possible I've been replaying a version of that afternoon in my head for six days, and that the version ossified somewhere around day two into something smoother and more final than what actually happened, something with a shape I preferred because it let me be injured instead of careless.

In any case I went to look at the dog. She had redone it on the heavy paper, and the muzzle was crisp now, each hair laid down separately with a 2H that barely left a mark, so that she'd had to go over it again and again, building value out of patience rather than pressure. The dark of the eyes was the only soft graphite on the page. It sat on the dark like a full stop at the end of a long sentence, and it was better than anything she'd drawn all year, and I told her so, and she said, "The stump's almost dead," and I said, "They wear out," and Rafael, from the wheel, said, "That's the denouement of the stump," and none of us laughed, but all of us almost did.

Mr. Lim came by during the last twenty minutes, hands behind his back, and stood over my stairwell for a long time. He is a man who can make silence feel like a weather system. Then he said, "The smudge here, at the base of the railing. On purpose?"

I looked. There was a smudge, a real one, my own palm ghosting up from the bottom corner where I'd been gripping the sheet, and for three weeks I'd read it as atmosphere. I'd been so careful with everything else, H pencils for the far wall, HB for the concrete, a 4B only inside the shadow under the third step, and my hand had betrayed all of it at the last possible place. I could erase it. Or I could decide it belonged, the way a room belongs to the person who has walked through it.

"I don't know yet," I said.

Mr. Lim nodded once, which could have meant anything, and moved on toward Madelaine's table. She had her pencil laid flat against the paper, dragging the whole side of the lead through the black of the dog's eye, and he stopped behind her with his hands still folded, and waited to see what she would do next.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
Cohen would like it recorded, first of all, that he was in the library entirely of his own free will, and not because Sana had texted him nine times, and certainly not because the ninth text said "I know you're reading this." He was there because he loved learning, a claim he repeated to himself as he climbed the stairs, and which he intended to keep repeating until it felt less like a lie.

Sana and Harmony had colonized the table by the window, which was strewn with an alarming quantity of paper for a Tuesday. "You're late," Sana said, though he was four minutes early, which he pointed out, and which she waved away like smoke. Harmony slid a photocopied page across to him, a passage from Jane Eyre, and beside it a worksheet with the depressingly clinical title "Applying Critical Lenses."

"Mr. Khoury wants two lenses by Thursday," Harmony said. "I'm doing feminist. Sana's doing Marxist. You're doing both, apparently, because you weren't here to defend yourself."

"I was here in spirit," Cohen said. "My spirit is very punctual." He read the passage, in which Jane speaks of her restlessness, her want of exercise for her faculties, and he read it again, and something in it snagged. "Okay, so with the feminist lens, she's arguing she needs more than the domestic sphere allows. That part's straightforward. But she also talks about women being just as men are, needing exercise for their powers. Is that a universal claim about human beings, or a claim about women specifically, and does the distinction matter?"

"It matters," Sana said, with the serene confidence of someone who had decided it mattered ten minutes ago and would defend that position to the death or until lunch, whichever came first.

"You're lionizing her a little," Harmony said, tapping the page. "She's a character, not a saint. Brontë gives her a speech and then marries her off to a man with a locked attic. The lens is supposed to ask what the text does, not what we wish it did." Cohen conceded this with the grace of a connoisseur being told his favourite wine was overpriced, which is to say he frowned and did not concede it at all.

That was when he pulled out his grandmother's copy, the actual 1890s edition with the cracked spine he'd taken from her house on Sunday. He'd found the title page confusing enough to photograph it, and now he set his phone on the table. "Look at this. Currer Bell. Who's Currer Bell?"

Sana leaned in. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which didn't reveal the author was a woman. It's in the footnotes of my edition. You didn't read the footnotes?"

"I read the important parts," Cohen said, wounded, and privately resolved to read every footnote of everything for the rest of his life, a resolution he estimated would last until Thursday.

Harmony was quiet for a moment, which was unusual enough that both of them looked up. "So the feminist lens," she said slowly. "The book is a woman writing as a man so that the woman's argument gets heard at all. And the Marxist lens is class, right, Jane's a governess, she's paid to be educated but belongs nowhere. Both of them are about who gets to speak and who has to borrow a voice."

Cohen looked at the phone, then the passage, then the worksheet, and felt the two lenses click together in a way he distrusted immediately, because feelings of click were historically unreliable. "That's it, though. Brontë uses a man's name, Jane uses standard English instead of her own plain speech when she needs authority, and the question underneath both is whether the borrowed voice changes what gets said." He paused. "Or whether I'm being facetious and stretching two lenses over one book like a bad bedsheet."

"You're stretching," Sana said. "But keep going. Stretching is the assignment."

Mr. Khoury drifted past their table on his orbit of the room, paused, read the worksheet upside down with the unnerving skill of long practice, and said only, "Footnotes, Cohen," before continuing on. Cohen stared after him, half convinced the man had read the text from Sana's apartment through several walls.

He wrote at the top of the page, in handwriting that would embarrass him later: borrowed voices, whose benefit? Then, underneath: uncertainty: does the pseudonym strengthen the argument or hide it? He underlined nothing, which for him was restraint.

"Mr. Khoury," he called across the library, and every head turned, including two belonging to people he had not known were there. "If I can't decide between the two lenses, is that a failure or a thesis?" Mr. Khoury considered him from a respectful distance and said, "That depends on whether you can hold both at once," and kept walking, and Cohen wrote that down too, under the uncertainty, with a small star beside it. Sana reached over and drew a second star. "For symmetry," she said.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Connecting words such as Spanish 'sin embargo', meaning 'however', let a debater signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of their grammar is simple.
story:
The sign-up sheet went up on Monday: five minutes, in Spanish, on a current issue, no notes. Mr. Zhao had taped it beside the door of room 114 with a single line under the title, which meant the assignment was not optional. Olivier wrote his name third, below Hafsa, who had written hers in green ink and then boxed it twice, the way she boxed everything she intended to win.

The issue he drew from the envelope was the four-day school week. He could argue either side; Mr. Zhao had made that explicit. What Olivier could not do was argue it in Spanish for five minutes, because his Spanish consisted of present-tense verbs, a small hoard of nouns, and the sentence patterns from two years of worksheets about a fictional family that ate dinner at eight. He had three days.

Hafsa was in the library on Tuesday with her laptop open and a stack of printed articles, because she did not trust screens during preparation. She wanted the top slot in the class ranking, which Mr. Zhao kept quietly on a clipboard and which she had held since October. Her topic was public transit funding. She had already drafted an introduction, and when Olivier leaned over she tilted the screen away, not rudely, just finally.

"How do you even link the arguments?" he asked. "In Spanish. Mine sounds like a list."

"Then make it a good list," she said, and turned back to her screen.

He tried that night. Four-day week: saves money. Four-day week: longer days. Parents need childcare. Teachers like planning time. He read it aloud in his room and heard what it was, a pile of stones with no mortar. His father passed the door, heard the halting Spanish, and offered, from the hallway, the name of an app. Olivier declined. He had never been an autodidact; he learned from people, from rooms, from being corrected in real time, and the app's patient blue owl felt like learning from nobody.

On Wednesday he stayed after class and asked Mr. Zhao to listen to his draft. Mr. Zhao listened all the way through, hands flat on the desk, and then said only, "Notice where you stop and start." He would not say more. He was like that about the debate unit; he graded it in silence, pen moving, and students had theories about why that none of them could confirm.

The noticing happened on the bus home. Olivier was watching two ninth graders argue about a game, in English, and he heard the shape of the argument rather than its content: one conceded a point before demolishing it. Yeah, the graphics are better, but. That but was doing all the work. The graphics are better was not his position; it was the other side's, borrowed for a moment, held up, and then set down. He got out his phone and looked for the Spanish for that move. It was two words. Sin embargo. However. He wrote it on his hand.

At home he rebuilt the argument around it. The four-day week saves money. Sin embargo, parents pay for childcare. The days are longer. Sin embargo, the students are tired. The grammar underneath stayed simple, present tense, subject verb object, the fictional family's dinner table, but suddenly the sentences faced each other. Each however turned the argument like a hinge, and he understood that a listener could follow the turns even where the grammar was plain, because the turning word carried the meaning of the turn. He did not need the subjunctive, which he did not have. He needed the hinge.

Thursday, the debates. Hafsa went second and was incisive, nearly fluent, and when the boy debating her tried to impugn her statistics she produced the source sheet from her folder and let it sit there on the table until he looked away. Mr. Zhao's pen moved. She came back to her seat with her jaw set like someone guarding a small lead.

Olivier stood third. The first minute was worse than his bedroom; his voice found the wrong vowel in escuela twice. But at the first counterargument he said sin embargo, and he heard the room shift, the slight straightening of the boy who had drawn the opposing side, because now there was something to oppose. He conceded the savings, however, and raised childcare. He conceded the long days could work, however, and pointed at the tired students in the rows in front of him, which got a laugh he had not planned and could not repeat. Five minutes. He sat down with forty seconds left on the clock and his palms damp against the desk.

Mr. Zhao's pen moved for a long time afterward, longer than it had for anyone except Hafsa. When the bell rang, Hafsa was already at the clipboard's shoulder, pretending to pack slowly, and Olivier heard her ask, "Is the ranking posted yet?"

"Friday," Mr. Zhao said, and closed the folder.

In the hallway she fell into step beside him. "You used the same word like six times."

"I know," Olivier said. "It's the only one I have."

She looked at him sideways, deciding something. "Transit funding has better ones," she said. "Dado que. No obstante." She held her hand out, palm up, waiting, and after a moment he took the pen she was offering and wrote both words on the back of his hand, under the first.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The quiz was first period on Friday, and by Wednesday lunch Edouard still could not make the derivative mean anything. He could compute one, dragging the exponent down and subtracting one, but the numbers arrived like freight at an unlabeled platform. Across the cafeteria, Neha was spreading her notes over two trays, and behind her the vice principal's countdown to the recycling bin's removal was taped to the pillar: two minutes, so the tables cleared fast, so everything mattered now or not at all.

"I don't get what the derivative is for," Edouard said. "I can find it. Then what?"

Neha pulled a napkin from the dispenser and flattened it against the table. "Ms. Whitehead said the sign of it tells you which way the function's going. Positive one way, negative the other." She drew a horizontal line and marked a point on it. "This is where it equals zero. Now test on either side."

Edouard took the pen. He picked a number left of the point, plugged it into the derivative he'd computed for his practice problem, and got a positive value. Right of the point, negative. "So it's positive here, negative there," he said. "That means the function rises and then falls."

"Which means," Neha said, tapping the marked point, "you've got a local maximum."

"A local maximum." He said it again, quieter, as though the phrase were a coin he was checking for weight. The bell shrilled; a monitor began expostulating at a boy who had wedged his tray into the bin at the wrong angle; the napkin had to be folded and pocketed like contraband. Edouard walked to fifth period with the crease running exactly through the marked point.

Here it must be said what the lunchroom could not show: that Neha, walking the same corridor, was not sanguine about her own understanding. She had explained the chart with confidence she did not fully own. In her mind the sign flip meant something about the graph turning over, a crest, and yet the phrase "because it rises and then falls" was hers only by repetition, borrowed from Ms. Whitehead's board and not yet tested against her own drawing. She wondered whether Edouard had noticed the half-second pause before she'd said "maximum." She decided he had not, and felt both relieved and slightly dishonest.

That evening Edouard sat at his grandmother's kitchen table while she told her long story about the mailman and the turkey, and he let her be a raconteur for a full ten minutes before he unfolded the napkin and smoothed it next to his homework. He redrew the sign chart larger. Positive on the left of the critical point, negative on the right. He sketched the function following those instructions: rising into the point, falling away after it. The crest of the curve sat directly above the marked value, and when he checked it against the answer in the back of the book, it matched. Not because a rule had been recited at him, but because he had watched the rise and the fall obey the signs, and the peak had appeared where they changed.

On Friday morning Serenity found him at the classroom door, holding his notebook like a shield. "Question four," she said. "The one with the cubic. Did you get a max or a min?"

"I got a max," Edouard said. "I made the sign chart. The derivative is positive before the point and negative after, so it rises and then falls, so the point is the local maximum."

Serenity frowned at her own paper. "I said minimum. I think I read the signs backwards."

"Test a number on each side," he said. "That's all I did." He wanted to tell her it was okay to get it backwards, that he had been backwards for two weeks himself, but Ms. Whitehead was already passing the quizzes down the rows, and the desks shuffled into their exam silence.

Serenity looked at him a moment longer, then pulled out her pencil and, on the margin of her quiz before turning it over, quickly wrote two small signs, one on each side of a dot.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
Morgan spread the two articles across the small cafe table like cards she intended to play against each other, though at the moment they lay there mutely, refusing to be played. One claimed that later school start times improved adolescent attention; the other, sampling different schools with different methods, found no effect worth mentioning. Her assignment, the first real one of a summer program she had talked her way into, was to write a critical review comparing them, and she had been avoiding it for four days by now.

She ordered a second coffee mostly to keep her seat honest. The cafe had the reliable hum of a Thursday afternoon, espresso machine exhaling, someone's playlist neither good nor bad enough to notice, and at the corner table Sophia was reading over a draft of her own review with the expression of a person trying to discernment her way through fog. Sophia was the reason Morgan was here at all; she had forwarded the program email with the message "you're smarter than me, do it with me, suffer with me."

"Listen to this," Sophia said, without looking up. "I wrote that the study's results were significant, so there's a ninety-five percent chance the hypothesis is true. That's what the p-value means, right? Like the study is ninety-five percent right?"

Morgan opened her mouth to agree, because it sounded right, because it was the kind of thing people said in class and nobody ever flinched. Then she closed it. She turned back to the first article, to the results section she had skimmed twice and understood once, and read the actual sentence, the one the number actually belonged to.

"Wait," she said. "I don't think that's what it says."

"It's what everyone says it says."

"That's not the same thing." She slid the article across the table. "Read the sentence. All of it. Slowly."

Sophia read it aloud, quietly, like someone defusing something. "The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect." She frowned. "That's backwards from what I said. It's the chance of the data being weird, not the chance the theory being right."

"Yes. Which is not the same number. Or the same idea. Or the same anything."

Sophia put her pen down. "So when I wrote ninety-five percent likely to be right, I was imputing a meaning to the number that it never had. I gave it a little coat to wear that doesn't fit it."

"That is a very forgiving way of putting it, but yes."

At the register, a woman Morgan knew as Ms. Karimi, who lived two doors down from her aunt and worked the counter on weekday afternoons, was wiping the milk wand and had, evidently, been listening, because she said, "Half my students get that wrong in the first week. Every year. Like a ritual." Morgan had known her for three summers and had somehow never learned what she taught.

"Statistics?" Morgan asked.

"Biostatistics. Twenty years." Ms. Karimi came over with a rag and, uninvited, sat down at the edge of their table, which felt less like intrusion and more like weather. "Don't worry, I'm not going to explain it to you. You already explained it to each other better than I would. I'll just tell you the twist."

"There's a twist?" Sophia said.

"There's always a twist." Ms. Karimi nodded at Morgan's laptop, which was open to Morgan's own draft, paragraph three, which Morgan had suddenly and privately gone cold about. "Go on. Read your paragraph out loud."

Morgan did not want to. She read it anyway, and there, in her own confident September-proof prose, was her own sentence: the study's findings were significant, suggesting the intervention was likely effective in ninety-five percent of cases, or something close enough to it that she felt her ears heat up. Sophia started laughing before Morgan even finished, laughing so hard she had to put her head down on the table next to the sugar caddy, and Morgan laughed too, mostly out of disbelief at herself, at the sheer gall of having corrected someone thirty seconds after committing the identical crime.

"I fixed yours before I fixed mine," Morgan said. "In my defense. Which is not a defense."

"It's a little bit of one," Sophia said, sitting up, wiping her eyes. "It's like catching a pickpocket and then finding the wallet in your own coat."

Ms. Karimi stood, taking her rag with her, but before she went she said, "The honest ones put the uncertainty in the review. The dishonest ones hide it. Guess which papers get cited more." Then she went back to the register, and a man with a stroller asked her something about oat milk, and she was absorbed into the ordinary afternoon as though she had never been a professor at all.

Morgan looked at her two articles again, the way she had at the start, but now they seemed less like opponents and more like two witnesses who had seen the same event from different windows. One study's methods were sounder; the other's sample was larger; neither had claimed, if she read the fine print honestly, more than the fine print allowed. The strange thing was that the p-value confusion, the thing she had gotten wrong, had actually sharpened her thinking about the comparison, because now she kept asking what each number was actually attached to, what claim, whose doubt, measured against what. She deleted her ninety-five percent sentence and, after a moment, deleted the whole paragraph around it too, which felt like pulling a thread and finding half the sweater attached.

Sophia leaned over. "So what are you going to write instead?"

"I don't know yet. Something about how the second study can't prove there's no effect, and the first one can't prove there is, and the review is where you say what you'd still want to know."

"That sounds like a C."

"It sounds like the truth," Morgan said, and typed: The evidence, taken together, is inconclusive.

Behind them the espresso machine exhaled again, and Sophia stole one of Morgan's sugar packets without asking.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Jessica had come to her grandmother's house because the Wi-Fi at home was down and Ms. Ho's assignment was due Monday: read the first chapters of Jane Eyre and argue something, anything, using either a feminist or a Marxist critical lens. She had voted for feminist without thinking, mostly because the word felt safer, something she could hold like a handrail. But her grandmother's kitchen table was wide and sunlit, and the novel was better than she'd expected, and by noon she was arguing with it out loud.

Kareem arrived at two with his laptop and a bag of chips, claiming he'd walk her through the Marxist thing because he'd done the reading twice. Denzel came an hour later, having given up on his own house. They spread the chapters across the table beside her grandmother's fruit bowl, where a plastic grapes arrangement from 1987 still beguiled visitors into reaching for it.

"Okay," Kareem said, and stood at the little whiteboard Jessica's grandmother kept by the phone for grocery lists. "Sort them. Every character." He drew a line down the middle and wrote OWNERS on one side and WORKERS on the other. "In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, like factories and land. The proletariat owns only its labour and has to sell it for wages."

"So Mr. Rochester goes on the left," Denzel said, naming the estate. "He's got the land, the house, the whole operation."

They filled the board slowly. Mrs. Fairfax, the housekeeper, went right, because she worked at Thornfield for wages even if she seemed genteel. Jane herself went right, then got a question mark beside her name, then an argument. Bessie the nurse. The servants. The Reeds on the left, the children inheriting what they hadn't earned. What bothered Jessica wasn't the sorting but how clean it looked, how the board made a house she'd been living inside all afternoon suddenly seem like a machine with a glass panel in its side.

"Try the feminist part on top of it," she said finally, and pulled the novel toward her. "Jane's a governess. She's a worker, she sells her labour, but she's also a woman being told her whole life what she's allowed to feel." She found the passage where Jane speaks of restlessness in the third storey, walking the corridors. "Look. She's not just poor. She's poor in a way that's supposed to be invisible. They dress her in black and expect her to vanish."

"The curtains," Denzel said, and pointed at the window where her grandmother's diaphanous white curtains shifted in the draft. "Like that. You can see through her, sort of, but she's still a barrier. She's furniture."

Jessica remembered, then, a thing from September: a group essay in Ms. Ho's class where she'd let a boy named on the roster as the first author though she'd written the thesis, and how she'd told herself it didn't matter. She had thought of it as politeness. Sitting here with the board full of owners and workers, she wasn't sure it had been. It might have been the same vanishing, done to herself, on purpose, and she disliked how easily the two explanations traded places. She wrote in her notebook that both readings could be true at once, and underlined it twice, then crossed out one underline because it looked too certain.

"The lie in it," she said aloud, testing, "is that the book kind of lets Rochester be complicated and romantic even though he owns everything, including, basically, the people in the house. That's the mendacity. Not him lying. The book lying about how charming that is." She heard herself say "kind of" and cut it when she wrote the sentence down. Ms. Ho wrote "vague" in the margins of anything softened.

Kareem pushed back gently. He argued that Jane marries money in the end, more or less, and that a Marxist reading has to reckon with that; Jessica argued that a feminist reading has to reckon with it too, and that maybe the fact both lenses caught the same scene in their glare was the actual thesis. Denzel said the question mark next to Jane's name should just stay there. They worked until the light went amber and her grandmother came in to peel potatoes, listening without interrupting, the way she did.

At the door, bags packed, Jessica took a photograph of the whiteboard before her grandmother wiped it for the grocery list. Jane's name with its question mark, left of nothing, right of nothing, holding both columns open. "I'm going to say in the essay that I changed my mind," she told them. "Started feminist, ended up somewhere wider." Denzel grinned and said, "Say you ended up a question mark," and she laughed and walked back in to help with the potatoes.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, and about 60 percent of that waste happened in households.
story:
Chase stacked the flour bins on the shelf at the back of St. Brigid's community kitchen and thought about the drawer in his mother's fridge. Last Sunday he had pulled out a bag of slimy spinach, a half loaf gone blue at the cut edge, and a carton of yogurt two weeks past its date, and he had stood there holding all of it over the compost bucket like a man weighing evidence. He had bought everything with a plan, or with something he had called a plan at the time, which turned out to be mainly optimism.

Ms. Petrov ran the Tuesday night class with a flat voice and no interest in being anyone's guru. "Six weeks," she had said the first night. "You will plan a week of meals, buy what the plan needs, cook it in batches, and eat what you cooked. If you waste less than you did before, you pass. I don't grade on charm." Gurshaan had leaned over to Chase and whispered that she was more drill sergeant than pedagogue, and Chase had said nothing, because from where he sat the two looked about the same.

The planning worksheet had columns for the day, the dish, the components, and the quantity, and Chase filled his out on the bus with a pen that kept dying. Chicken and rice on Monday, doubled so Tuesday was covered. Lentils Wednesday, since they kept forever and he could cook the whole bag. Thursday, the pasta his father made, which used the end of every vegetable in the house, whatever shape it was in. He wrote it out twice because the first version had him buying cilantro for one recipe, and he already knew how that story ended.

It was Gurshaan, of all people, who brought the number into the room. He was supposed to be pricing ground turkey on his phone, and instead he read out loud from an article he'd found. "A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022. And about 60 percent of that waste happened in households." He looked up. "Households. Like, us. Not restaurants, not factories. Regular fridges." Christophe said that couldn't be right, that surely supermarkets threw out more, and Gurshaan turned the phone around so he could read it himself, and for a minute the three of them stood there among the price lists doing the arithmetic in their heads. Sixty percent of a number that size, coming out of drawers like the one in Chase's mother's fridge.

Chase thought about that while he shopped on Saturday with the worksheet folded in his pocket. His father, when Chase had mentioned the class, had waved it off; in his house you bought what looked good and you cooked what you felt like, and throwing things out was just part of the rhythm, the way Sunday followed Saturday. His mother planned nothing and wasted everything, and her own mother, Chase knew from the stories, had kept a root cellar and a jar shelf and never lost an onion in her life. He had assumed the old way was sentimental and the new way was freedom, and now he stood in the produce aisle with two sweet potatoes in his hand, holding a position that belonged to neither of them. He put one back.

On Sunday he cooked in the community kitchen with five other students, four burners going, Ms. Petrov moving between stations. When he portioned the chicken and rice into containers, she stopped and looked at his tray. "Labeled?" He hadn't. She waited while he found the tape. At the station beside him a man his father's age argued with Christophe about whether cooked rice could go in the fridge warm, querulous now, softening when Christophe showed him the worksheet line for cooling time, and Chase watched the man's shoulders drop as if something in him had been allowed to rest. Small information, but it seemed to allay a worry the man had carried for years.

The week held, mostly. Tuesday's chicken became Wednesday's lunch because a friend from his floor knocked on his door at nine with a problem that took two hours, and dinner dissolved. Thursday the pasta absorbed the last of a pepper and half a wilting bag of arugula that would otherwise have followed the spinach into the bucket, and it was good, and he ate it standing at the counter feeling, for no reason he could defend, like he had gotten away with something. The lentils sat in their jar, untouched, because the plan had assumed a version of the week that did not exist.

Friday night he tallied it for Ms. Petrov. Two containers of rice gone fuzzy by Thursday, which he had cooked too much of, and one lemon, dried out on the sill, that no recipe had ever asked for. Everything else eaten. He wrote "wasted: rice, one lemon" on the worksheet and stared at the line. One lemon and some rice against a number with nine zeroes in it, sixty percent of it coming from rooms like this one, and he could not tell whether his small tally meant the problem was solvable or only that it was so large his part in it barely registered. He was starting college in a month, in a dorm with a fridge the size of a shoebox. He folded the worksheet along its creases and put it in his pocket, and then he took it out again and added, at the bottom, "smaller fridge, smaller list," and left it on the counter for Ms. Petrov to find in the morning.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
Noah had told his interview panel, twice, that the museum's DNA exhibit was basically memorized, and this was true in the way most of his claims were true: loosely, and with consequences arriving later. Ms. Bui had nodded, given him a lanyard, and assigned him the molecular biology wing, where the summer interns were expected to explain transcription and translation to visitors without notes. The internship itself, the one that actually paid, went to only one of the trainees, and everyone knew it would be decided at Saturday's evaluation, when each of them would be dropped into the wing with a live audience and judged from the mezzanine.

Saturday arrived smelling of floor wax and rain. Aiyana was already at the codon wheel when he came in, spinning it slowly with one finger, her lips moving. She wanted the internship more than she admitted; her mother had been laid off in March, and Aiyana had been taking the early bus all week to practice before the museum opened. Noah knew this because he'd been taking the early bus too, to spy on the competition, though he told himself it was dedication.

His own preparation had gone differently. He had memorized a speech, polished it in the mirror, and built it around a line he considered brilliant: every three-letter word in the DNA code means one amino acid, and the cell reads the message like a sentence with no wasted words. It sounded authoritative. He had not checked it against anything.

Visitors began to file in around ten, a family with strollers, a cluster of boys from a summer program, an elderly couple moving between exhibits like slow birds. Noah watched Ms. Bui take her place on the mezzanine with a clipboard, and then the tannoy crackled and his name was called first. The wing went quiet except for the hum of the double-helix model, four feet of glowing beads rotating on its axis.

He began well. He unwound the story the way the enzyme unwinds the strand, and when he reached the part about the code, he delivered his line. "Every codon, every three bases, specifies exactly one amino acid. One word, one meaning. It's the most efficient system in nature." A hand rose in the second row, a girl maybe fourteen, thick glasses, holding the museum's laminated codon chart the way other people hold maps.

"If it's one word, one meaning," she said, "why does the chart say all these different ones mean leucine?" She held it up. Six entries, six different three-letter combinations, all pointing to the same place.

The room's attention transfixied him; he felt it physically, a pressure behind the eyes. He could have said he didn't know. Instead, because his speech was all he had, he said, "The chart is simplified for visitors." The girl looked at the chart, looked at him, and said nothing, but a boy beside her was already counting under his breath, tapping each row.

From the mezzanine, Aiyana could see everything Noah could not: Ms. Bui's pen stopping mid-word, and the boy's finger moving down the full chart, all sixty-four entries, arriving at the number twenty, twenty amino acids, saying it out loud with mild surprise, "so there's more than twice as many codons as amino acids," and the girl frowning because she'd caught the adult in something and adults were supposed to be safe. Aiyana felt a complicated thing she could not have named, part vindication and part nausea, because she had found the same fact alone on Tuesday, spinning the codon wheel, and had spent an hour rewriting her own speech around it: most amino acids have more than one codon. She had assumed Noah knew it too. She'd assumed he knew everything; that was the trouble with the way he talked.

She watched Ms. Bui lean forward and write something long. She watched Noah try to recover, gesture at the helix, retreat to safer ground, the part about the message being carried out of the nucleus, the reading of it in threes, and she understood that whatever happened next, she was going to have to go out there in fifteen minutes and be better than a boy who was currently drowning, and that wanting this felt uglier up close than it had on the early bus. Her mother's face came to her briefly, utilitarianism in its plainest form, the greatest good for the smallest family, and she set it aside. There was also just the work, the wheel, the beautiful evanescent moment on Tuesday when the pattern had opened under her finger and then closed again like water.

When Noah came off the floor he was pale and quiet, and the girl with the glasses was still standing at the wheel, spinning it, watching the letters cycle. He went over to her. "I was wrong," he said. "I'm sorry. I should have checked the chart instead of trusting my speech." She shrugged, the way fourteen-year-olds shrug, and kept spinning, and after a while she said, "It's kind of better this way, isn't it? That it's not one word, one meaning." Noah looked at the wheel, at the sixty-four windows cycling past, most of them pointing to one of only twenty places, and heard the tannoy say Aiyana's name.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
Olivia had carried the chocolate in her pack for two days wrapped in a towel, and by the time they reached the campsite it had bloomed into something grey and streaked, like a window in an old house. She set the pot on the camp stove anyway. Her grandmother had taught her to bake in a kitchen with a marble slab and a proper thermometer, and Olivia had watched her the way an acolyte watches, hands folded, memorizing. What she remembered most was the snap. You could hold a tempered square to your ear and break it, and it sounded clean.

Graham had brought a thermometer, a cheap digital one he used for brewing coffee. He handed it over without being asked. "If you ruin my chocolate, I'm telling everyone it was you," Olivia said, and he shrugged, laconic as always, and went to collect firewood.

She melted the dark chocolate first, stirring over the low flame, watching the numbers climb. That part she knew. You brought it up hot, then cooled it while you worked it, folding and folding on the overturned pie tin she'd brought as a slab. The dark set in streaks and then in one even sheet, and when she cracked a corner off, it snapped. Ophelia, who had been slicing apples at the picnic table, looked up at the sound.

"Okay," Ophelia said. "That's actually satisfying."

The milk chocolate was the problem. Olivia ran it through the same steps, the same numbers, the same patient folding, and it refused. It stayed wet-looking at the edges, and where it did firm up it bent instead of snapping, dull as candle wax. She tried again with the last of Graham's bar, and again it smeared under her thumb.

Mr. Wright, who ran the campsite store and had come by to see whether they needed propane, stood at the edge of the firelight and watched her scrape the tin. He was not a man who explained things. "My sister does that," was all he said. "The wedding favours. She swears by a notebook." Then he walked back toward the store, and his flashlight bobbed away between the tents.

Olivia sat on the picnic bench with the failed chocolate cooling beside her and pulled out the notebook, though it was her grandmother's, copied out in her own handwriting before the old woman's hands got too uncertain to write. She turned pages of temperatures she had transcribed without understanding, columns for dark and columns for milk, and there it was, plain as a shopping list: milk chocolate was tempered lower, around 29 to 30 degrees Celsius, while the dark numbers she had used ran hotter. No reason was given. Just the numbers, in her grandmother's round, patient hand, beside a note that read "milk fat." Olivia read it twice. She had run the milk chocolate up to the dark chocolate's temperature and held it there, and it would not set because she had been working it too warm.

By the third attempt her fingertips had been in and out of the melted chocolate so many times that they had desensitized to the heat, and she trusted the thermometer instead, stirring and cooling, cooling and stirring, watching the display fall degree by degree until it read 30. She spread it thin. They waited. Ophelia whittled the point off a stick and Graham fed the fire, and nobody said anything, which Olivia understood as a kind of manners.

When she broke the corner piece it snapped, and the surface caught the firelight and gave it back shiny. Ophelia put a piece on her tongue and closed her eyes. Graham took two pieces and ate them one after the other, which from Graham was a speech. Olivia wrote the numbers again in the back of the notebook, dark and milk in separate columns, and under milk she added a question mark, because she still did not know why the two could not share a temperature, only that they could not. She put the notebook in her pack, zipped it, and held the last square out toward the dark, where Mr. Wright's porch light burned yellow past the treeline.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
The gym smelled of varnish and old mats, and the basketball hoops had been cranked up to the ceiling like surrendered flags. Cole set a folding table at center court and laid out fourteen pennies and one nickel, because he had exactly fourteen actors and one lead, and because he had read, three nights running, the paragraph in Ms. Byrne's directing book that had rearranged his whole understanding of the job. The word blocking, the book said, came from nineteenth-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. He had a miniature stage now, roughly, taped out in blue painter's tape on the table's surface, and the coins were his blocks.

He also had a problem, which was that his two best friends disagreed about everything. Kayden, who played the older brother in the one-act, believed a director should tell people exactly where to go and let the feeling follow. Arnaud, who played the Ferryman, believed you should let actors find their own movement and merely watch, like a birdwatcher unwilling to disturb the birds. Cole had tried both methods in the two weeks since Ms. Byrne had handed him the play and the gym keys and the sentence, "The interregnum between the old director graduating and the new one arriving is yours, if you want it." He wanted it. He just did not know yet what kind of director he was.

On Monday he had ruled the floor like Kayden. He walked actors through their positions like a drill sergeant, and the scene ran clean and dead, the lines landing with the flatness of recitation. On Tuesday he surrendered to Arnaud's method and let the actors wander wherever instinct carried them, and by the end of rehearsal the Ferryman was standing behind the sofa, hidden from the audience, delivering the play's most important speech to a brick wall.

So on Thursday, he set out the coins.

"Sit," he said, and Kayden and Arnaud sat on the bleachers while the other actors stretched and whispered. Cole slid the nickel along the taped floor of the table. "This is you, Kayden. You enter here, door left. And when Marisol says she's leaving, you don't go to her." He moved a penny, not the nickel. "She comes to you. She crosses to center because she's the one choosing."

"You're doing it with money," Arnaud said, leaning over the table, close enough that Cole could smell the noxious energy drink he'd had at lunch. "That's a thing. That's an actual thing."

"It's where the word comes from," Cole said. "Gilbert. W. S. Gilbert, nineteenth century. He planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. Blocking. I read it in Ms. Byrne's book."

"So it's not just a made-up job," Kayden said slowly, picking up the nickel and turning it over. "People have been doing this with little figures for over a hundred years."

Cole shrugged, though his pulse had lifted. "They've been planning. Like a battle, or a dance."

He had not felt that lift before this week. There had been a moment, two summers ago at drama camp, when the student director of his group had swept the lunch table clear and laid out quarters and dimes, sliding them through the salsa and around the napkin dispenser, saying "you go here, you go there," and Cole, thirteen and standing on a cafeteria bench to see, had felt something open in his chest like a window. He had forgotten it until Monday night, flipping through the book and hitting the word Gilbert. Then the memory came back whole: the coins, the model stage, the director's total calm. He had gone looking for his own fourteen pennies the next morning, emptying his father's change jar onto the kitchen counter while the coffee maker gurgled.

Rehearsal began. Cole placed the actors where the coins said, then did what Arnaud had taught him, which was to watch. When Marosal's sister, played by a girl named in the program only as the Neighbor, kept drifting upstage, he saw why: the folding chairs for the audience were stacked wrong, and she was steering away from their noxious smell of disinfectant. He moved the chairs. When Kayden delivered the reconciliation speech, Cole noticed that the blocking had left him stranded too far from Marisol, and rather than shout a correction, he called a five-minute break and tried it on the table first, sliding the nickel and the penny together until they touched.

By eight o'clock the run-through worked. Not perfectly; the lights still flickered whenever someone kicked the extension cord, and the curtain, a borrowed bedsheet, undulated in the draft from the propped door like something alive and impatient. But the scene breathed. Kayden reached for Marisol at the exact moment the table had predicted, and Arnaud's Ferryman crossed downstage in a slow diagonal that Cole had never planned and would never have dared to invent, a movement that made the whole gym seem suddenly larger.

Afterward, Arnaud and Kayden waited by the table while the others gathered their bags. Kayden spun the nickel. "So which one of us was right?"

"I don't know," Cole said. He looked at the coins scattered across the tape, at the little distances between them, some of which the actors had honored and some they had found their own way across. "Both. Some of it I planned, some of it they found, and I can't always tell anymore which is which."

Arnaud picked up the penny that was Marisol and set it back in its shoebox, in the slot lined with felt where Cole kept them between rehearsals. "Do it again tomorrow," he said. "With the felt box. And bring more pennies."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The chemistry wing of the science museum smelled faintly of hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Eric had been standing in front of the same exhibit for eleven minutes. It was a sealed glass tube inside a small heating chamber, its liquid a pale straw color, with two brass buttons labeled WARM and COOL. Beside it, a placard explained that the liquid contained a dissolved compound that reacted reversibly with itself, that the forward reaction absorbed heat, and that the product was deeply blue. Luca had read the placard once, at speed, and was already bored.

"Okay, so," Luca said, jabbing a finger at the glass. "You warm it. Which way does it go, bluer or clearer? Ten bucks."

"Bluer," said Flora, who had arrived at the museum late and out of breath, her museum pass still folded in her fist.

Eric leaned closer. He was doing this chapter in school right now, Le Chatelier's principle, and Mr. Shin had made them copy the statement into their notes twice, in pen, no cross-outs. He turned the sentence over in his head the way he turned over anything he half-knew, testing which side of it was load-bearing. A change imposed on a system at equilibrium shifts it to oppose the change. Warming the tube was the change. Opposing it meant pushing back against the added heat, which meant going the direction that soaked heat up. The forward reaction absorbed heat. So the forward direction was the one that drank warmth out of the liquid, and feeding more warmth in would feed that direction. "Bluer," he said. "It goes toward the products."

"No way." Luca folded his arms, doing his belligerent posture, the one he saved for arguments he suspected he was losing. "Heat is like a product of any reaction that warms up, everyone knows that. You add a product, it goes backward. Clearer. It's basic."

"Then press the button," Eric said.

Luca pressed WARM. The chamber hummed, and for a long moment nothing happened, long enough that Luca started to grin. Then the color moved through the liquid the way dusk moves through a room, not all at once but unmistakably, and the tube stood there deeply, seriously blue. Luca stared at it with his mouth slightly open, as though it had cheated.

"Ten bucks," Flora said, palm out.

"I don't have ten bucks. I spent it on the parking meter. I am a person of no solvency whatsoever until Friday."

"That's a loan, then," Flora said, and Luca paid her in the coin of a groan.

Eric kept his hand near the COOL button without pressing it. He wanted to see the other half of it, the return trip, because in his experience a thing you had only seen once you did not actually know. He pressed it, and they watched the blue thin out gradually to straw, and he felt the small private satisfaction of a prediction that had survived contact. But it also bothered him that Luca's version had sounded reasonable. Luca's version had a logic to it, just the wrong logic, and Eric could not quite articulate where the seam was between the two, the exact step at which plausible became false. He understood the rule well enough to bet on it and not well enough to teach it, and he was honest enough with himself to know those were different things.

Mr. Shin, it turned out, was two exhibits over, filling out an evaluation form for a field trip he was planning for his junior class. He drifted toward them with the mild unhurried air of a man who collected observations the way other people collected receipts. "Ah, the equilibrium tube," he said. "You've discovered it heats blue."

Eric explained, carefully, what he had worked out, that opposing added heat meant favoring the direction that absorbed it, and the forward reaction absorbed heat, so warmth pushed the reaction toward the products. Mr. Shin nodded but said nothing further, which Eric had learned was how Mr. Shin confirmed you had something right; the man saved his speeches for wrong answers, and even then they were short.

"There's another tube like this in the storeroom," Mr. Shin said. "Broken heater. If the museum ever asks me, I'll say the exhibit should be a pair, one you can warm and one you can only cool, so visitors see both directions. Nobody ever believes one direction until they've seen it reversed." He tapped the glass once with his knuckle, a small sound, like knocking politely on a door.

"I still say it's backwards," Luca said, though without heat now, more like a man filing a dissent he intended to drop. "You got lucky."

"Then watch," Eric said, and pressed WARM again, and they stood together in the dim chemistry wing, three of them and a teacher, waiting for the blue.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of 1 over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves.
story:
The corner store smelled of cardamom and floor wax, and Nevaeh had claimed the stool behind the counter as hers for three summers now, so Ms. Holloway let her spread her calculus notebook between the register and the jar of pickled eggs. Rain came down in ropes against the window. She had a quiz tomorrow and one problem refused to behave: the integral of one over x, from two to eight, and every attempt she made collapsed.

She tried the power rule first, because the power rule had carried her through October. Add one to the exponent, divide by the new exponent. But one over x was x to the negative one, and when she added one to negative one she got zero, and dividing by zero left her staring at a page of nonsense. The rule that had felt like a skeleton key turned out to have a lock it simply could not open. She wrote the failed attempt out again, slower, as if her handwriting were the problem, as if the equation were obdurate only because she had approached it rudely.

The bell over the door rang and Jawad came in shaking water off his jacket, on his way home from the tutoring centre two blocks over. He bought a bag of salt and vinegar chips and leaned on the counter instead of leaving. "You look like the math is winning," he said.

"It's not math," Nevaeh said. "It's this one function. The power rule dies on it. And the tutor centre closes at six, so." She turned the notebook so he could see the wreckage.

Jawad crumpled the chip bag slightly, thinking. He had sat through the same unit, and something had survived the sitting. "There's a special case," he said. "For exactly this. Our teacher called it the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x. That's the antiderivative for one over x." He said it the way you recite an address you looked up once and never needed again, and she could tell he did not know why it was true, only that it was.

Nevaeh wrote it down. Then she tested it, because a formula you do not test is a formula you are merely obeying: she took the derivative of the natural log of the absolute value of x, in her cramped marginal script, and got one over x back. It checked. The logarithm slid into the gap the power rule left like the one puzzle piece that had been sitting under the couch the whole time. She computed her area, two to eight, got the log of eight minus the log of two, and felt something settle that had been rattling all evening.

She sat with it, though, because it bothered her a little, too. All through school the rules had been presented as if they were complete, and this one had a hole in it, patched by a function from a family she had been told was separate, a different drawer entirely. Her father, when she'd complained about the tutoring centre fees, had called her education an investment, as if the whole thing were an externality he was absorbing for the family's future good. She had smiled at the word then. Now she understood the sentence differently: the cost was real and it was hers as much as his, and what it bought was not a finished structure but a better map of what she did not know. She could predicate her confidence on the power rule for months and never once learn where it failed. That was the part that stung. She liked believing in complete rules.

Ms. Holloway came out from the back with a crate of tinned tomatoes and set it down between them. "Locking up in ten," she said, and then, seeing the notebook, "Did you solve your little mountain?" She meant the graph, the curve Nevaeh had sketched a dozen times, the region shaded like a hillside on a map.

"I got the area," Nevaeh said. "But I can't explain yet why it's a logarithm and not something cleaner. I can verify it forward. I can't build it from nothing." She closed the notebook and slid it into her backpack, the zipper catching on the corner of a folder, and Jawad held the door while Ms. Holloway turned the sign and killed the register light. Outside the rain had thinned to a drizzle, and the streetlight made a long yellow smear of the puddle at the curb. "Tomorrow," Jawad said, "ask the tutor why." Nevaeh pulled her hood up and stepped into it.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
Ms. Aziz had said the assignment was due Monday, and I had said, sure, no problem, I would do it Friday night, which is why the folder of printed population pyramids was in my backpack on a camping trip I had told Cristina I absolutely did not want to go on. That part is true. The part where I claimed Darian begged me for three days is not, or not exactly; he asked once, by text, and I packed the folder anyway, which tells you something about which of us actually wanted me there.

The first night we got the fire going and Darian told the story of the canoe that was not actually his canoe, and Cristina, who is voluble after ten at night in a way she never is in a classroom, kept interrupting him with corrections, and I sat with the flashlight under my chin reading the pyramid for Japan and pretending I was somewhere quiet. The pyramid is just two bar graphs turned on their sides, facing each other, males on the left, females on the right, and the bars at the bottom were fat and the bars at the top were thin, which I already knew from the diagram Ms. Aziz had put on the board, so I moved on to Nigeria, where the bottom was enormous and the whole thing narrowed fast toward the top like an actual pyramid, the kind you draw in second grade.

The question we had to answer was this: given the shape, will the country need more schools or more nursing homes. That was the whole assignment. It seemed too easy, which made me suspicious of it, the way I get suspicious of Cristina when she is being nice to me for no reason.

I got it wrong first. On the Japan pyramid I noticed that at the very top, the oldest group, the right side was wider than the left, and I decided it must be a printing error, because I could not think of any reason the two sides would differ, and I wrote in the margin, in pencil, "smudge??" Cristina looked over my shoulder while I was writing it and asked what a smudge was doing at the top of a bar graph, and I said I did not know yet, which was at least honest.

The next morning it was raining, so the four of us, counting Ms. Aziz's neighbour's dog that had followed us up from the trailhead, sat under the tarp and Darian played cards with Cristina and I lined up the pyramids in a row across the picnic table, Japan, Nigeria, Italy, Brazil, and checked the tops of all of them. Every one. The right side wider at the top, every single time, males left, females right, I had not mixed up the sides. I did not have signal, so I could not look it up, and Darian said maybe it was a coincidence, and I said four out of four is not happenstance, and he said fine, then what is it, and I said I still did not know.

What I did, and I want to be accurate about this because Cristina claims she said it first and she did not, is I transliterated the problem. There was a note in the margin of my notes from class, in Ms. Aziz's handwriting, that said "the top of the pyramid is the oldest group," and I had been reading it as a label, but if the top is the oldest group, then the right side of the top is the oldest women and the left side is the oldest men, and if there are more of the women, then the answer is not that the graph is smudged. The answer is that the women are still there.

Darian guessed it before I said it out loud. He said, "Women live longer than men, on average," and I checked it against all four pyramids and it held, and I said so, and Cristina said she had been about to say that, which is the kind of thing she says, and I let her have it, because being right felt like enough.

So then the assignment opened up in a way I had not expected. For Nigeria, the answer was schools, obviously, the base was so wide that you could see the classrooms from orbit. For Japan, the answer was nursing homes, and not just any nursing homes, because of the top of the pyramid, more of the oldest people were women, which meant the need was shaped a particular way, and I wrote that down, and then I sat there feeling like I had solved it and like I had not solved it at the same time, because the pyramids only tell you the shape of the population and not what the country can afford, or chooses to build, or whether the grandchildren stay or leave for Lagos or Tokyo, and none of that is in the bars.

I want to say I thought about all of that under the tarp in a thoughtful and organized manner. What actually happened is the rain stopped and Cristina dragged us down to the lake and I left the pyramids weighted under a thermos, and it was not until we were carrying the canoe back, the real one, the borrowed one, that I decided what I would write: schools for Nigeria, nursing homes for Japan, and a paragraph saying the pyramids are honest about the shape of a population and silent about everything else, and that the top-heavy right side tells you the oldest old are mostly women, and that this is a real fact and not a smudge.

Cristina asked me on the drive home if I thought Ms. Aziz would mark me down for the last paragraph, the uncertain one. I said I did not care. Then I took the folder out of my backpack at the gas station while Darian paid, and I crossed out "smudge??" so hard the pencil went through the page.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In the Jewish Passover tradition, the festive meal is called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning 'order', because its rituals follow a fixed sequence from start to finish.
story:
The community hall smelled of burnt soup and lemon polish, which was, Ashton decided, an honest summary of the whole enterprise. His grandmother's Seder notebook lay open on the folding table, its margins crowded with her handwriting, some of it in Hebrew, some of it in a shorthand that had died with her. His father had handed it over in March with the ceremony of a man passing on a crown, and also the relieved grin of a man handing off a chore. "You're the eldest grandchild," he'd said, as if that explained anything. "You'll figure it out." Six weeks later, Ashton had figured out exactly one thing: the order of the steps mattered, and he did not know the order.

Moshe arrived first, carrying a grocery bag of matzah like a man transporting dynamite. He set it down and peered at Ashton's stack of index cards, which were shuffled, written in two colors of pen, and numbered in a system that had already collapsed. "This is a mess," Moshe said, with affection. "You've got the handwashing after the sandwich. That's a war crime." Kaitlyn came in behind him with a stack of Haggadot, the little booklets she'd photocopied at the library, and she fanned them out on the table like a card dealer. "I read all thirty pages last night," she announced. "I understood maybe nine."

Mr. He, who ran the hall's Thursday night kitchen and had let them rehearse there in exchange for leftovers, drifted over with a tray of plastic cups. He was circumspect about other people's religions, but not about other people's table settings, and he adjusted their centerpiece twice before saying anything. "You have done this before, yes?" Ashton admitted he had only ever sat at the table, the youngest grandchild for years, asking the Four Questions on autopilot while thinking about the brisket. Now his grandfather's chair was empty and somebody had to sit in the front of the room instead, and that somebody kept losing his place.

They did a full run-through after sundown, or a partial one, because Ashton lost the thread somewhere between the bitter herb and the matzah and improvised a lengthy blessing that was, Kaitlyn whispered, mostly the rhyme scheme of a commercial jingle. "The whole point," she said, tapping her photocopy, "is that it's called a Seder. That's a Hebrew word that means order. The festive meal follows a fixed sequence from start to finish, that's why it has the name." Ashton stared at the fifteen steps listed on the inside cover of the booklet, which he had somehow never read because it was the inside cover of the booklet. "It's in the front of the book," he said. Moshe patted his shoulder. "Many important things are in the front of books. You are not the first to skip them."

He recopied his index cards that night at the hall's long table, one step per card, numbered, in a single pen. It was not the copying that helped, though; it was the discovery that the order was not a cage. The songs came at the end, after the meal, when everyone was loose and full; the questions came at the beginning, when everyone was still hungry and attentive; the wine, the washing, the story, the food, each thing placed where it would land best. His grandmother's messy margins, he realized, were not mess at all but a working record of someone who knew the structure so well she could decorate it. He had been trying to memorize her flourishes before learning the building.

The real Seder arrived with thirty-one relatives, two folding chairs short, and a cousin who spilled grape juice on the good tablecloth before the first blessing. Ashton stood up, felt every eye, and did not faint. He led the candles, the wine, the handwashing; he pointed at his nine-year-old cousin for the Four Questions and mouthed the first words to help her; he watched his father's face do something complicated and warm during the story of leaving Egypt. When he paused at the sandwich step, unsure, his aunt called out "korech" from the third row like a stage prompt, and he laughed, and the whole table laughed, and he continued. After the meal, when they reached the songs, his uncles sang loudly and badly, and the bathos of it, a roomful of grown adults bellowing "Had Gadya" with goat noises, felt less like a failure of solemnity than like the point.

Later, stacking chairs while Mr. He mopped, Ashton thought about how he had wanted, at first, to abrogate the whole thing and beg his father to lead it, and how glad he was that he hadn't, and also about the questions that still sat uneasily in him, chiefly the one about his grandfather's chair, which no amount of correct sequence would fill. He didn't say any of that out loud. Kaitlyn was gathering the photocopies into a crooked pile, and Moshe was eating leftover charoset straight from the bowl with a serving spoon. "Same time next year?" Moshe asked, mouth full. Ashton looked at the notebook, now rubber-banded and safe in his bag, its margins still waiting to be added to. "I get the good chair," he said, and dragged another chair onto the stack.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: For the same sample size, a poll's margin of error is largest when opinion is split near 50 percent, and pollsters usually report that largest figure.
story:
The survey had seemed like the easiest assignment of the term: write five questions, poll the class, present the results. Charlotte had predicted nothing but an afternoon of tally marks, and yet here she was, third period on a Thursday, staring at two numbers that refused to mean the same thing.

"Nineteen out of twenty-one said the fall festival should keep the bonfire," she told Jonathon, spreading her sheets across the desk beside his. "And then look at this one. Ten said the festival should move to the football field, eleven said keep it in the quad. Eleven to ten. And the margin of error Mr. Njoroge gave us is the same for both. Plus or minus something like twenty-one percent. How can that be right?"

Jonathon leaned over the papers with the air of a boy who had learned to check her work before agreeing with it. "Maybe he photocopied the same table twice."

Presley, who had been drawing a small fire in the corner of her notebook, looked up. "Twenty-one percent would swallow your whole eleven-to-ten vote, wouldn't it. That's not a margin, that's a mouth."

Mr. Njoroge was circulating between the desks, pausing at each group long enough to ask one question and no more, which Charlotte had come to think of as his teaching style and his personality at once. When he reached them, he tapped the nearly unanimous sheet with one finger and said, "Same sample size, same margin of error. Interesting, no?" and moved on before she could ask the question that was already forming, the way questions did with him, like a cough you had to hold until he was out of range.

Charlotte sat with it. She turned both sheets face up and looked at them the way she looked at proofs when the obvious step hid from her, sideways. Nineteen out of twenty-one was almost everyone. Eleven to ten was almost nobody deciding anything. Same class, same twenty-one people, same error. Which meant the error couldn't be about how split the answers were, or the unanimous one would have had almost none. So what was it about? She tried, briefly, to predicate the whole margin on sample size alone, the way the worksheet implied, and that worked, but it left a strange taste: it meant the twenty-one percent described the worst case, the question where the class was cut exactly down the middle. She checked the split question again. Ten and eleven. As close to half and half as twenty-one people could get.

"Wait," she said. "I think the margin of error is biggest when it's near fifty percent. Like our bonfire-location vote. And when it's nearly unanimous, it's actually smaller. But pollsters report the biggest one anyway, the fifty-fifty number, because that's the safe thing to print."

Presley frowned. "So my bonfire drawing is safe, but the location vote tells us nothing?"

"It tells us the class can't make up its mind, and now we can prove it can't." Charlotte laughed, surprising herself. "We surveyed everyone and learned that we know nothing. That might be the most honest thing a poll has ever said."

For the presentation, she made two posters. On the first she wrote the bonfire result with a fat confident arrow, nineteen of twenty-one, no caveats; on the second she wrote the location result and above it, in letters large enough to read from the back row, PLUS OR MINUS MORE THAN THE DIFFERENCE. Jonathon suggested she also draw the mouth swallowing the vote, and she let him, because the incipient chaos of their poster session was already attracting attention and a small cartoon margin eating a ballot box could only help. When her turn came, she explained the unanimous question quickly, then held up the split one and said only, "Both of these have the same margin of error, because the margin depends on the sample, not the split. It's biggest near fifty percent, and that's the number we report, even for questions like this one, where it's overkill."

A hand went up in the second row. "So which do we actually want, the field or the quad?"

Charlotte looked at her poster, at the tally marks that had cost her a week, at the number that had turned out to be a kind of ceiling rather than a verdict. "I genuinely don't know," she said. "We could ask more people. Or we could ask better questions. Or we could accept that some classes stay split and the committee just picks." She rolled the posters and tucked them under her arm. "Raise your hand if you want the field."

Eleven hands. She counted them twice.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
Annabelle had chosen the article because it was short, and now she suspected that shortness was a trap. It ran to six paragraphs in Spanish, printed from a newspaper website, and described a change to the voting rules in a small town where voters without certain documents would be turned away. Her task, for Thursday's seminar, was to read it and then summarise it aloud in her own words, also in Spanish, for ninety seconds without notes. She had two evenings left, and she had spent the first one on the last paragraph.

That had seemed sensible at the time. The final paragraph was the shortest, only three sentences, and she had hoped to finish it quickly and bank a small victory. Instead she had spent forty minutes on a quotation from a retired postmistress, full of subjunctives and an idiom about doors closing, and when she finally understood it she realized it told her almost nothing: the postmistress thought the change was a shame. That was all. Annabelle sat in her bedroom with the dictionary open on her knees and felt the whole evening dissolve behind her like heat off a road.

At lunch the next day she spread the article out on the library table between Amira and Kelsey. The fourth floor of the library was the quiet floor, and the shelves near their table held the foreign periodicals, a display that had looked moribund since before either of them had started at the school, its magazines fanned and faded under fluorescent light. Kelsey was meant to be studying for chemistry. Amira was meant to be doing nothing in particular, which she did with great commitment.

"I can read it," Annabelle said. "Mostly. It's just, when I try to say what it's about, everything I decoded turns out to be the wrong part. That quote took me an hour and it's nothing. The whole back half of the article is nothing."

Amira pulled the page toward her, though she studied Italian, not Spanish, and scanned it with the confidence of someone who could not be embarrassed by a language she didn't speak. "This first paragraph, though. Look how dense it is. It's got the town, the rule, the date, how many people, everything crammed in there. Why would they do that?"

"Because readers give up," said a voice behind them. Ms. Joshi was shelving returns two aisles over, and she set down her cart and came to the end of their table. She did not sit, which was how they knew she would not stay long. "Inverted pyramid," she said. "That's what my old editor called it. Most important facts first, details after. The opening paragraph carries the core story." Then she straightened a chair that did not need straightening and went back to her cart, and that was the entire speech.

Annabelle looked down at the paragraph she had saved for last, having assumed it would be the hardest, and read it again. It was the hardest. It was dense, clotted with clauses, and it was also, now that she looked, the whole article in miniature: the rule, the vote, the number of people who might be turned away. The postmistress was decoration. The details she had spent an hour on were the loose gravel at the bottom of the pile.

"I've been reading it backwards," she said. She heard how obvious it sounded and said it anyway.

"Entropy," Kelsey said, not looking up from her equations. "Any system left alone, that's what happens. You went for the easy disorder first." It was the most she had contributed to a conversation in a week, and Annabelle decided to take it as affection.

She spent the lunch hour on the opening paragraph alone, and it was slow, but it was slow the way climbing is slow rather than slow the way wading. There was a sentence about the town council's vote, and beneath it, in smaller type, a phrase she could not crack, something about those the new rule would disenfranchise, voters who lacked the papers the council now demanded. She wrote the phrase on her wrist, then thought better of it and wrote it in her notebook, because summarising aloud with writing on your wrist was a bad plan even by her standards.

On Thursday the seminar met in Ms. Joshi's room, but the projector was broken, so they walked down the hall to the library instead and crowded around the low table by the periodicals. Two classmates went first and both faltered, one of them standing with his eyes shut, visibly trying to remember the exact wording of the final paragraph, and Annabelle watched him do it and felt a small private gratitude toward him, the way you feel toward someone who tests the ice ahead of you.

When her turn came she began with the core, in her stiff but serviceable Spanish: the town, the vote, the number of people. She got the number slightly wrong, said three hundred instead of three thousand, and corrected herself, and no one laughed. The details she offered after that were thin, and she left out the postmistress entirely. Ninety seconds, when she sat back down, had not even fully elapsed.

Afterward Amira leaned over. "You skipped the quote. I liked the quote."

"I know," Annabelle said. "That's the part I actually understood." She turned the page face down on the table, then turned it over again and folded it into her notebook, unresolved, the way the town's argument was unresolved, the way she was not yet sure whether a summary that loses the doors closing is a smaller truth or just a truer one.
