Kelsey, packing up, pointed at the faded display on the wall and said, "They should throw those out," and Ms. Joshi, from behind the desk, said, "Leave them. They're the only ones who still come here on Thursdays."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
I have never been sure whether Ms. Hu actually said it, or whether I needed her to have said it and so invented the memory afterward, the way you invent a stash of money in a coat you have already checked twice. This is the problem with being me: I narrate my own life a little too well, and some of the narration is at odds with the record. But on election morning, the record itself was thin. I was eighteen and eleven days, I was registered for nothing except my dorm room in September, and Klara was leaning in the doorway of my bedroom holding her voter card like a boarding pass.

"You're coming," she said. Not a question. Klara asked questions when she already knew the answers she wanted.

"I'm not on the list," I said. "I never did the registration thing. My mom said they'd mail something. Nothing came."

Klara looked at me the way she looked at the impecunious kids in our economics textbook, the ones used as examples of things that happened to other people. "So you're just not going to vote in your first election."

I told her I'd walk with her anyway. The polling station was in our old high school gym, which felt like a joke the universe was making at my expense: six years of sitting on those bleachers, and now I'd return as a citizen and be turned away at a folding table. In grade twelve, Ms. Hu's civics class had run the whole spring around the election. She refused to tell us how she voted, which at the time I thought was cowardice and now suspect was the entire point. One gray afternoon, someone's cousin had asked, through this someone, whether you could still vote if you'd missed every deadline, and I remembered Ms. Hu saying, "You can register at your assigned polling place on election day." Plain as that. Whether she said it to me or to the room, whether it was March or May, whether the someone was Kathy, I honestly cannot swear. My memory confounds me more than any statistics unit ever did; Ms. Hu taught us that word, too, a confounder being the hidden third thing that makes two true facts lie to each other. My hidden third thing, that morning, was shame.

The gym smelled the same, wax and dust and old popcorn, and the election workers had set up their tables where the badminton lines crossed. A woman with a lanyard asked for my card. I said, too fast, "I'm not on the list, I never registered, is that, can I still." I had rehearsed it and the rehearsal fell apart anyway.

" ID with your address?" she said. I had my driver's licence and a hydro bill my mother had thrust at me with the vehemence of a woman indemnifying herself against all future blame, as if by handing me the envelope she had transferred every consequence to my own account. The woman copied something down, had me sign a line in a book, and said, "There, you're registered," with less ceremony than the librarian used for overdue returns.

That was it. No gate, no penalty, no dramatic third act. Klara was already at the screen, and I followed her and stood behind the little cardboard booth and found, to my irritation, that my hand was not steady. Four years of Ms. Hu asking us to separate what we wanted to be true from what we could argue for, and here I was with a pencil and a circle, wanting to be the kind of person who voted on principle and suspecting I was the kind who voted on spite, which my mother would call the same thing.

I marked the ballot. I folded it in thirds, because everyone ahead of me had folded it in thirds, and slid it into the box, where it made no sound at all among the others. Klara caught up with me outside the gym doors, in the corridor where the trophy case is, our grade ten relay trophy still in there with my name misspelled on the plaque.

"Same as your mom?" she asked.

I hadn't decided yet what to tell her, or my mother, or myself, and I said so, and Klara laughed. We pushed through the doors into the parking lot, past the woman from the folding table having a smoke against the brick, her lanyard flipped over, the October light flat on the windshields, every car holding somebody who had made the same small mark I had, or a different one.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
Gabrielle spread the graph on the towel and weighed its corners with shells because the wind off the water kept lifting it like something that wanted to leave. She had until Monday. Ms. Somsak had handed back the quizzes on Friday with a red circle around the number forty, and Gabrielle had folded the paper into eighths and pushed it to the bottom of her bag, where it sat all weekend like a subpoena she refused to open.

"You're doing homework at the beach," Mederick said. He was standing calf-deep in the surf, letting the waves argue with him.

"I'm doing the beach at my homework," she said. "There's a difference."

Karen dropped onto the far end of the towel, sandy and dripping, and looked at the graph over Gabrielle's shoulder. It showed a line climbing steadily upward across decades, small jagged teeth along its length like a saw. "That's the carbon dioxide one," Karen said. "The saw-tooth part is the seasons, I think. Mederick, come sit down, she's going to fail."

"I'm not going to fail."

"You got a forty."

Gabrielle flattened the paper against her knee. The problem, she had decided on the drive here, was not the line. The line went up; that much was obvious even from a distance. The problem was the left edge, where the line began, because Ms. Somsak's retake question wanted the starting value and then how much it had risen since, and Gabrielle had skipped the first part entirely on Friday, racing for the answer without ever finding where the story started. She traced the axis now with one finger, down and left, until the finger stopped at the first point.

"Okay," she said slowly. "The first reading. Mauna Loa, March 1958. About three hundred and thirteen parts per million."

"What does that even mean," Karen said, "parts per million?"

"Like a fraction of the air. Out of every million molecules, three hundred and thirteen of them were carbon dioxide back then." She said it and waited to feel uncertain, but it held. She had read that section four times last night without it sticking, and now, with the graph in front of her and the numbers actually under her hand, it held.

"Fine," Karen said. "Now the other half. Why does it matter? That's where you lost points. You wrote like two sentences."

Gabrielle looked out at the water. A man farther down the beach was adjusting an umbrella, patient under the full sun, and she watched him for a second while the right way of saying it assembled itself. "Sunlight comes through the atmosphere and warms the ground, and the ground gives heat back off," she said. "The carbon dioxide doesn't block the sunlight coming in, but it traps the heat trying to get out. So more of it means more heat stays." She picked up a handful of dry sand and let it run. "It's like a blanket. Thin blanket, some heat escapes. You keep adding layers."

"That's actually good," Mederick said.

"Don't sound surprised." But she was testing it against herself, the two halves of the question she had always kept separate, the graph and the mechanism, the number and the reason for the number, and for the first time they fit together in one piece. She still couldn't have said exactly why parts per million, of all the ways to measure a thing, was the way scientists had chosen, and she said so out loud, because pretending otherwise had cost her before.

By late afternoon the wind had gone soft and the tide had come up and taken the dry strip where Mederick had been standing. Gabrielle was quizzing Karen, making her find March 1958 on the axis, making her say the number back, when a woman walking the wet sand slowed near their towel. She wore a sun hat and a canvas bag and had been there, Gabrielle realized with a slow cold drop in her stomach, for the whole last hour, seated on the next blanket over behind the windbreak, close enough to hear every word.

"Nice explanation," Ms. Somsak said. "The blanket part especially. Though you left out where the saw teeth come from."

"Monday," Gabrielle managed. "I have until Monday."

"I know." Ms. Somsak lifted her bag onto her shoulder and looked once at the graph, at the climbing line, at the small jagged teeth. "I was here first."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
The public library smelled like carpet cleaner and old paper, and the computer Jason wanted, the one by the window with the good GIS software, was taken by a man watching fishing videos with the sound off. Jason stood behind him for a minute, weighing the ethics of loitering, until Ms. Berg appeared at his shoulder and said, "The lab has six terminals free. Follow me." The lab was a room he'd walked past a hundred times, thinking it was for staff. It had a poster of a topographic map of the county with a pin in it that said YOU ARE HERE, which was technically true of everyone in the building.

He'd started the project because of Uncle Ray's new house. Uncle Ray had shown everyone the listing at Thanksgiving, a pale-blue ranch near the river, and had said, "One percent flood chance a year, that's nothing," and everyone had nodded, and Jason had nodded too, and then at home he couldn't leave it alone. He'd run the numbers three times on scrap paper before bed, expecting to be reassured, and instead the math had come back the same every time: a home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once over 30 years. Thirty years was a mortgage. Uncle Ray was signing a mortgage. Jason had texted him and gotten back a thumbs-up and the words "thanks, buddy," which is what Uncle Ray said when he wasn't listening.

So now Jason was in the library lab learning to layer a flood risk map over a housing map of the city, because one fact about one house felt like a splinter and he wanted the whole board. Ms. Berg showed him the toolbar once, told him the software was "older than you but loyal," and left him alone in a way that felt like a compliment.

Skylar found him an hour later, sliding into the next chair with a slushie the size of a fire hydrant. "What are you doing on a Saturday. Voluntarily. At the library." Jason tilted the screen. The map of the city hung there in two skins: underneath, the housing stock, each parcel shaded by year built; on top, translucent blue, the flood zones, and where the two layers overlapped, the blue sat on the oldest houses like water actually rising. "Watch," he said, and toggled the flood layer off and on. Skylar stopped chewing her straw.

"That's the east side," she said. "Andrew lives over there." Andrew lived, according to the map, in a shallow bowl of blue that Jason had not been able to unsee since he'd found it. He was going to have to decide whether to tell him, and he already knew he would, and he already dreaded it, because there was no way to say "your neighborhood floods" that didn't sound like you were the one deciding it.

When Andrew came in, damp-haired from the bus, Jason showed him without preamble, because Andrew hated preamble the way other people hated mosquitoes. Andrew leaned in, squinted, and did the thing Jason least expected: he laughed. "Yeah, dude. We know. My grandma's sump pump has a name. We call it CaptainNemo." He pointed at the screen. "Half those houses, the people there can't sell and can't move, so they just stay and pump. You think you're the first person to discover water?"

Jason felt the rebuke land somewhere between sting and relief. He had been walking around with the map like it was a secret he'd uncovered, and here it was the weather of other people's whole lives. "I'm not trying to be an apologist for the zoning or anything," Andrew went on, tapping the blue. "Whoever let them build cheap housing in the cheap land, that part's pernicious, honestly. It's just not news to us."

They worked for another hour, all three of them, and Skylar turned out to be annoyingly good at the software, finding a slider that let them shade parcels by median value so that the whole city sorted itself into an argument you could see. In the overlap zones, the values dropped, and Jason understood something he couldn't yet say out loud: the map didn't just show where water would go. It showed where money had already gone, decades ago, and the water was just following the money downhill. When he tried to explain this, Skylar said, "So the rich people bought the hills a hundred years ago and cauterized the whole thing with a zoning code, and now the map is the scar." That wasn't quite what Jason meant, and it was also better than what he meant, which was typical.

The catch, the part he kept circling, was the uncertainty. The flood layer was a model, and models were built from the past, and everyone said the future didn't respect that. He couldn't overlay "the future" on anything. He could say a house in the zone had about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once across a 30-year mortgage if the yearly chance stayed at 1 percent, and past that he was guessing like everyone else. He wrote that caveat on a sticky note and put it on the monitor, where it curled at the corner like it wanted to escape.

Ms. Berg came by at closing and looked at the map for a long moment, hands in her cardigan pockets. "You going to do something with this, or just know it?" Jason said he'd emailed Uncle Ray the actual numbers, no spin, and told him to ask about elevation certificates before the closing. Uncle Ray had replied with a question mark, then, twenty minutes later, "ok what's a 30 year flood chance again?" and Jason had typed out the whole thing patiently, one percent a year, about twenty-six percent over the mortgage, and pressed send. Then he'd sat there hoping it was the kind of knowledge that helps, suspecting it might be the kind that just sits in your uncle's phone.

The lights in the lab clicked to half, the library's way of saying go home. Skylar copied the project file to a drive and tossed it to Andrew, who caught it and held it up to the window, the little rectangle outlined against the parking lot. "For the pump guy," Andrew said. "CaptainNemo's getting a map."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
Coralie found the letter taped to her locker on the last morning of exams, the envelope so florid with glitter that it shed onto her sleeves when she peeled it off. Inside, in Lydiane's looping hand, was an invitation to the pre-graduation dinner her family was throwing at the restaurant on River Street, eight o'clock, everyone welcome, no gifts, which everyone understood to mean gifts. Coralie held the envelope for a long moment, because Lydiane's family had money in the quiet way that didn't need to announce itself, and her own mother had spent the spring recalibrating every budget in the apartment after the pharmacy cut her hours. She decided to go anyway. She would bring something small, and she would not apologize for it, which was a discipline she had been practicing like scales.

The day passed in the usual rituals of departure. In the west hallway, seniors were signing the margins of a mural of a whale that some graduating class had painted years ago and no one had ever repainted. Rian was squatting by the whale's tail with a marker, and when Coralie crouched beside him he said, without looking up, "My dad keeps asking what the diploma's actually worth. Like, in money. He thinks I should've done the trade program." Coralie said she didn't know, and the honest blankness of it stayed with her through lunch, through the last walkthrough of the gym where the chairs were being set in rows, through the moment Mr. Kowalski stopped her by the doors and told her that her essay on duress and consent in the Antigone unit had been the best thing he'd read in ten years of teaching it. She thanked him and felt the strange split of the day, being praised and uncertain at once.

At the dinner, Lydiane's grandmother held court at the head of a long table, and somewhere between the appetizers and the main course a great-uncle leaned toward Coralie with his glass raised. "Do you know what that piece of paper is worth?" he asked. "In 2023, workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma, the median was eight hundred ninety-nine dollars a week. Without one, seven hundred and eight." He sat back, pleased with himself, as though he had handed her a coin. The table murmured its approval of arithmetic. Lydiane rolled her eyes across the tablecloth at Coralie, a small conspiracy of embarrassment.

But Coralie didn't feel embarrassed, or not only. She felt the numbers settle somewhere and begin to work on her. A hundred ninety-one dollars a week, and she did the multiplication under her breath while pretending to listen to a cousin describe a gap year in Lisbon, and the annual figure assembled itself, ungainly and real. That was the median, she thought, which meant half were below it, which meant the number was a crowd and not a promise. She looked down the table at Rian, who was stacking sugar packets into a ziggurat, and thought of his father, who was not wrong to ask what things cost. She had spent the spring irritated at adults for talking about money when she wanted to talk about everything else, and now, uncomfortably, she could see both positions at once, the way you see both the vase and the two faces.

"Excuse me," she said to the great-uncle, louder than she'd meant to, and half the table turned. "Is that per week, full-time?" He said it was, median weekly earnings, 2023, ages twenty-five and up, and he repeated the figures as though she hadn't been listening. "No, I was listening," she said. "I just wanted to know exactly." Something in her voice made Lydiane's grandmother laugh, a short, delighted bark, and say, "Good, ask exactly," and the conversation broke apart into smaller, warmer channels.

Afterward, in the parking lot under the string lights, Coralie found Rian sitting on the curb with the last of his cake. She sat down even though her dress was not a curb dress. "Your dad asked what the diploma's worth," she said. "It's worth a hundred ninety-one dollars more a week, median, for people twenty-five and over. That's real. I looked at it the whole dinner." Rian turned the numbers over, fork stopped in the cake. "But that's everybody," he said. "Not me." "Not you," she agreed. "That's the part I can't fix. It's a true thing about a crowd and it says almost nothing about either of us." He laughed then, the first real laugh of the evening. "You're going to be unbearable in college." "Probably," she said. "But I'll be well-paid and unbearable, medially speaking."

Her mother picked her up at eleven, and in the car Coralie recited the numbers, not to impress but to place the fact between them like an object they could both hold. Her mother was quiet for two blocks, then said the diploma was worth more than that to her, and Coralie said she thought both things could be true. She watched the streetlights pass. Graduation was in two days, and she still didn't know what she would study, or whether the money would hold out past the second year, or how to be a person who counted things and a person who refused to be a total of things at the same time. But she had asked exactly, and the world had answered with something partial and honest, and that felt like a way of standing in it. Her mother pulled into the lot, and Coralie got out carrying her shoes in one hand and the glitter-shedding envelope in the other.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent: plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent.
story:
The group chat had been named "Newsroom" by someone optimistic back in September, and by October it had become the place where Ashton, Marie-Pier and Serenity argued about headlines at eleven at night while pretending to do homework. Tonight the argument was about a poll. The student council election poll, forty respondents, that the paper was going to run on Friday. Ashton had the draft open on his laptop, phone face-up beside it, the chat ticking upward.

"Read the caption again," Serenity typed, then, before he could: "'Mairie-Per leads Doyon 58 to 42, with a margin of error of 3 percent.'" She followed it with a single period, which from Serenity meant fury.

Marie-Pier, who had written the caption, defended herself in lowercase. "it's 3 percent. that's what mr. bekele's sheet said."

Ashton read the sentence four times. Something about it snagged, the way a sleeve catches on a door handle, and he sat back to cogitate. He was good at this part, the slow part, the part Serenity called "staring into the middle distance like a Victorian ghost." He did not mind. Ghosts, in his experience, were usually right.

"but 3 percent of what," Serenity typed. "of the 58? that's like 1.7"

That was it exactly, Ashton thought. That was the snag. The draft said three percent, and Serenity had just read it as three percent of the fifty-eight, because that was what the words meant, and if that was what the words meant then the whole number wobbled differently. He typed: "i don't think that's how it works. i think bekele meant points."

"points," Marie-Pier sent back. "points of what"

Ashton got up and paced his bedroom, which took four steps in each direction, his socks catching on the nail the landlord refused to fix. His father called from downstairs to ask if he was okay. "Fine," Ashton called back, which was his answer to everything, and sat down again.

He opened the draft in editing mode and typed a reply to the chat: "ok so look. plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent." He stared at it, deleted "ok so look," restored it, deleted it again, and sent it bare. "points. not percent."

There was a long pause, the kind where he could picture Marie-Pier rereading. Then: "wait so it's 3 percentage points"

"Yes," Ashton typed. "percentage points. it's its own thing." He could hear Mr. Bekele's voice saying it, that one line from Tuesday's class, tired and precise: "A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent." Ashton had written it down at the time mostly because Bekele had repeated it, and teachers only repeated things that showed up on tests or in life.

Marie-Pier was typing for a while. "so if i wrote 3 percent, and someone did 3 percent of 58, they'd get a way smaller number. like the poll would look way more precise than it is."

"basically," Serenity sent, adding, "ashton you can say basically you're not on the record."

But Ashton was not finished, because the more he turned it over, the more the caption bothered him in a second way. Forty respondents. Forty. He typed: "also bekele said the margin of error depends on sample size. forty people. what's the margin even doing on forty people."

"making us look official," Marie-Pier typed.

"making us look fake official," Serenity typed.

Ashton laughed out loud, alone, at half past eleven, and his father knocked once on the ceiling with something soft, possibly a slipper. He pulled the sheet Bekele had handed out from his binder, flattened it under the desk lamp where the light was warm and the laminate made the page nearly impermeable to highlighter, which he knew from experience. The sheet gave a margin for a sample of four hundred, not forty. There was nothing on it for forty. Forty was, he suspected, a number where the honest answer was "we asked the people who were standing near the cafeteria door on Tuesday."

"maybe we run the poll without the margin," he typed. "just say forty people, here's what they said."

"then it's not a poll it's gossip," Marie-Pier typed.

"it's a poll of forty," Serenity typed. "ashton's right. we either say what we actually know or we dress it up."

Marie-Pier did not reply for a long time. The chat showed her typing, then not, then typing again, the little bubble appearing and vanishing like something surfacing and deciding against it. Ashton watched the bubble and ate the last of the cereal from the box beside his keyboard, dry, without milk, because the milk was downstairs and the stairs were far.

"i'll rewrite the caption," she finally sent. "points. and the range. and i'll ask bekele tomorrow about the forty."

"good," Serenity sent. "also ashton is a misanthrope but a useful one"

Ashton typed "i like people fine, i just like them at a distance of forty respondents" and then deleted it, because it was funnier unsent, and because Marie-Pier had already posted the revised caption: "Mairie-Per leads Doyon 58 to 42 among 40 respondents; with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points, her likely range is 55 to 61 percent." He read it twice. It was correct. Whether it was honest, with forty people, was a different question, and it was eleven fifty-two, and the poll would run Friday either way.

"asking bekele at lunch," Marie-Pier sent. "you're coming."

Ashton looked at the time, then at the empty cereal box, then at the blinking cursor in the caption field, where the number forty sat between the words "among" and "respondents" like it had nothing to hide.

"fine," he typed. "lunch."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item, so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one.
story:
Ashley had promised herself she would learn to code before college, and now she sat in the last row of the camp's only air-conditioned room, staring at a laptop that belonged to the library and smelled faintly of somebody else's sunscreen. On the whiteboard, Mr. Weiss had written a game: think of a number between one and a hundred, and guess it. Bodhi, beside her, shouted "seven" immediately, the way he did everything, and Mr. Weiss just said "higher," and then "higher," and then "lower," until Bodhi had burned through nine guesses. Alana, two seats over, whispered something to Ashley and then raised her hand. "Seventy-three?" she asked. "Lower." "Fifty-two?" "Higher." "Sixty-two?" "That's it." Three guesses, and Mr. Weiss clapped twice, which was apparently his version of applause.

Afterward he showed them the trick written out. If the numbers were sorted, you could jump straight to the middle item, check it, and throw away half the list every time. He called it binary search, and beside it he wrote linear search, which was what Bodhi had done, checking items one at a time from the start. Ashley copied both words into her notebook, and then, because the afternoon workshop was self-directed and she wanted something to show for the summer, she decided she would build the fast one herself.

The project came from the camp itself. The director kept a running list of every camper's name for the daily raffle, and every morning some counselor had to find one name on a list that had grown past four hundred entries, drawn up in whatever order kids had registered. Ashley volunteered to write a program to do it. She had learned about linked lists that first week, because they were what she could manage: each entry holding a name and a pointer to the next, a chain she could add to anywhere without shifting anything. It had felt clever then, like hiding cards up a sleeve. She spent Tuesday sorting the list alphabetically, working through dinner, and Bodhi brought her a plate with the pizza crusts cut off, which was his way of saying he noticed she hadn't eaten.

Wednesday she wrote the search. It was short, almost insultingly so. Look at the middle item, she told the computer; if the target comes before it, search the front half; if after, the back half; if equal, announce victory. She tested it on a list of ten names, then a hundred, and the program found "Ferreira, Marta" in what felt like no time at all. She stood up so fast her chair scraped, and Alana came over, and they high-foured, and Ashley said, "I beat the counselors, I beat all of them."

But she wanted proof. The camp kept the old paper records from previous summers in a crate, and on Thursday she typed in eight hundred more names until her list held over a thousand, perfectly sorted. Then she timed it. Then, for comparison, she timed the old way, a linear search that started at the first entry and walked forward name by name. She ran each one ten times and wrote the averages on the back of her hand.

The numbers were nearly identical.

She ran it again, and again, and the binary search never pulled ahead, not even on a thousand names, and she sat there with her thumb still warm from the stopwatch feeling like she had been let in on a joke whose punchline nobody would tell her. She drew it on paper. Middle item. To look at the middle item, she had to go to the first item, then the second, then the third, and keep going until she reached the middle, one entry at a time, exactly what the slow search did. Her clever data structure, the one that made inserting a name so easy, was charging her a toll for every single step in the middle, and she paid it over and over each time she cut the list in half. She had not built the fast thing. She had built the slow thing wearing the fast thing's name.

She found Bodhi at the lake during free swim and explained it with a stick in the sand, drawing boxes and arrows. He squinted at it, skipping stones between questions, and when she got to the part about walking to the middle, he stopped skipping. "So the list eats your speed," he said. "It eats my speed," Ashley said, and laughed, and then didn't, because it stung a little. Alana found them there and listened to the whole explanation twice, then asked the question Ashley had been circling: whether it was worth rebuilding the whole thing, copying the names into an array where you could jump anywhere at once. That was Friday's problem, and Ashley didn't know yet. The linked list was still better at adding names mid-morning when the late campers arrived, and she would have to give that up, and she hadn't decided whether the speed was worth the trade.

At the evening raffle the director pulled a name from a coffee can, the old way, paper folded twice, and it was Bodhi's. He whooped and chose the cosmopolitan bag of foreign candy from the prize shelf, peeled a purple wrapper off something labeled in Dutch, and handed the first piece to Ashley without being asked, cataloguing aloud the tiny peccadilloes of the taste while campers threw ping-pong balls around them. Ashley held the candy in her mouth and watched Mr. Weiss across the room marking attendance off a printed list, starting at the top and moving down one line at a time, and she took out her notebook and wrote: middle item, then, underneath, walking. On Monday she would start the rebuild, she thought, or maybe she would keep both and let the linked list handle the mornings. She closed the notebook and went to claim her second piece.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
Tyson spread his notes across the kitchen table until they crowded the salt shaker and the dish rack, and then he set the balance scale beside a gallon zip bag full of white powder and a small bottle of vinegar. Ms. Ngo, who had taught chemistry at the high school for thirty years and now lived two houses down, had lent him the scale with a look he chose to read as faith in him rather than pity. On Thursday he had gotten a 61 on the stoichiometry quiz. The problem had asked for the moles of carbon dioxide produced from a given mass of baking soda, and he had frozen, the numbers sliding away from him the way they always did when it mattered.

Rhea arrived at four with her own textbook under her arm and no greeting, because they were past greetings. "Did you weigh the bag first?" she said, pulling out a chair.

"142.6 grams. Bag, soda, vinegar, all sealed inside. I put the vinegar in a little cup so it wouldn't mix yet."

"Then tip the cup over and seal it fast."

He did. The bag fizzed and strained and went taut as a drum, and he stood there with his hands hovering, some old instinct insisting that the swelling had to mean new matter, that something had been created out of the churning. The scale read 142.6 grams still. He tapped the display, weighed it twice more, and the number sat there, obdurate, refusing to change by even a tenth.

"That can't be right," he said. "Look at it. It's about to pop."

"It's right," Rhea said. "The law of conservation of mass. The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system. Ms. Ngo drilled that into us sophomore year. You were drawing on your shoe."

He had been drawing on his shoe. He remembered that year as the year his father had left the second time, and chemistry had seemed like a foreign country he had no passport for, and Ms. Ngo had written "Tyson can do this" on a returned quiz in red pen, a sentence he had folded small and kept in his wallet like recompense for everything else. He had never decided whether to believe it. Believing it felt like a risk, since if he tried in earnest and still failed, there would be nothing left to blame.

He sat down and pulled the quiz toward him. Mass of reactant, molar mass, moles. "Okay," he said slowly. "So the grams of baking soda I start with, that all goes somewhere. Nothing vanishes. If I divide the mass by the molar mass, I get moles of soda, and the reaction map tells me how many moles of gas come out of that. The gas was in the bag the whole time, it just wasn't gas yet."

"Where does the mass go when it becomes gas?" Rhea asked, testing him.

"Nowhere. It's the same mass. It's just sequestered in a different arrangement until the reaction lets it out." He was talking fast now, the way he did when something assembled itself ahead of his ability to write it down. He worked the original quiz problem again from the top, converting grams to moles, carrying the ratio across, and got an answer that matched the key at the back of the book. Then he did the next one without the key and could not check it, and did a third, and his hand cramped and he kept going.

Keith banged in through the side door looking for the good extension cord, saw the swollen bag on the scale, and said, "What's it supposed to do, explode?"

"It's supposed to weigh the same," Tyson said. "That's the whole point."

Keith squinted at the number as if it were withholding something from him personally, took the cord from the drawer, and left. Rhea laughed, and Tyson laughed, and then it was quiet except for the fizz dying down inside the bag.

He looked at his three worked problems, the third one still unverified, the answer possibly wrong, possibly fine, and he could not tell which without turning the page. He thought about Ms. Ngo writing that note two years ago, betting on a kid who had given her no evidence, and about how the bag on the scale had held its number through all that commotion. He picked up his pencil again. "Give me one more," he said. "Hard one."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
story:
The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered phone repair shop, its window papered with posters of places Arianna had only ever seen in Mr. Diallo's slideshows. She had come in for the poster of Japan, the one with the bullet train threading past a mountain, but she stayed because of the pyramid taped beside it, a chart shaped like an hourglass turned on its side, wide at the top, narrow at the base. Hasan had told her about these before the exam, and she had nodded and memorized the bars and then forgotten them, the way she forgot anything learned only to be graded.

"You're the third person this week to stand there," said the man behind the counter, who wore a name tag with a company logo and nothing else she could read. "Exchange program?"

"September," Arianna said. "Eleven months. My grandmother keeps asking whether I'll be safe, which is not, I think, the real question."

The man pulled a brochure from under the counter and slid it toward her. Inside was a second pyramid, the same shape as the poster's, and a caption she read twice. Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, it said, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s. She had assumed old was a relative thing, a shade of comparison. Twenty-nine was not a shade. It was a fact you could hold.

She thought of her own street, where the school at the corner had put a trailer in the parking lot for the overflow of grade nines, and where the retirement home further down had a waiting list her aunt had joined two years ago. Two buildings, two shapes. She had never once considered them as a pair, as a question a government might have to answer with a budget line. A wide base meant classrooms. A wide top meant something else, and she felt the odd vertigo of realizing that a chart on a wall was really a forecast of cranes and construction, of one kind of building rising while another fell quiet.

The door chimed and Emrick came in, still in his uniform from the shift at the grocery store, ebullient as always, talking before the door had finished swinging. "Tell me you're not doing homework in a travel agency."

"It's not homework." She turned the brochure toward him. "Look at the top of this. Nearly a third of the country is sixty-five or older."

Emrick leaned on the counter and studied it with the unembarrassed attention he gave to bus schedules and box scores. "So it's like, a country full of my grandma."

"She hates when you compare things to her."

"She'd like Japan, then. Everyone there is her." He grinned, then let the grin fade into actual thought, which was rarer and, she had to admit, more interesting. "Wouldn't that change everything, though? Not just nursing homes. Buses. Stairs. How fast people walk."

"That's what I keep landing on," Arianna said. "We learned these pyramids as if the point was reading the shape. But the shape is just the beginning. The shape tells you what a whole country has to build, and what it can stop building."

The man behind the counter, who had been listening with the tolerance of someone paid to be near conversations, cleared his throat. "My wife's from Nagoya," he offered. "We go back most summers. First time I visited, I counted the schools we passed and the care homes. I couldn't tell you the numbers now. I just remember which list was longer."

Arianna copied the figure into her notebook, 29 percent, 65 or over, early 2020s, and beneath it she began to collate what she knew, which was not much and yet more than she had known an hour ago. The trailer in the school parking lot. The waiting list. The man's two lists. Hasan's memorized bars. She was trying to hold the demographic fact and the lived fact in the same hand, and they fit together badly, the way a map of floodplains and a photograph of one flooded kitchen fit together badly, each true, neither containing the other. She could predict a country would need more of one building than another. She could not predict what it would feel like to live among the buildings, and she wrote that in the margin, honest, unhelpful.

"Mr. Diallo would say you're overthinking a poster," Emrick said.

"Mr. Diallo would say it's metonymy, probably. The chart standing in for the country. He loves a word like that." She closed the notebook. "But it isn't standing in for anything. It's just a count. The standing-in is what I'm doing."

They walked out into the late afternoon, and Arianna stopped on the pavement, the brochure rolled in her hand like a small tube. In eleven months she would be inside the shape she had been studying, riding trains past buildings she could now guess at, sitting in classrooms whose numbers she had, until today, never thought to wonder about. She would learn the answer to a question the chart could only pose. Emrick tugged her sleeve toward the bus stop, and she followed, still holding the rolled page, the way the figure 29 sat in her memory, exact and, for now, weightless.

"Arianna," Emrick said, when they were halfway to the corner, "when you're there, count the schools too."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States.
story:
The laminated map covered most of the kitchen table at his grandfather's house, curling at one corner where the kettle's steam had softened it. Jesse weighted the corner with a jar of pickled onions and ran his finger down the eastern edge of the United States, stopping where the warm water bent away toward the open Atlantic. Tomorrow morning he had to stand in front of Mr. Reddy's class and explain, in four minutes, how the ocean kept Europe warm, and tonight he still could not make the map say anything back to him.

The deadline had been set a week ago, and Mr. Reddy had not softened it. "Four minutes, no notecards," he'd said, tapping the sign-up sheet. "You'll explain a current of your choosing and take questions." Syed had chosen the Humboldt Current because he liked saying it. Lucille had taken the Kuroshio and then spent three days trying to convince Jesse to trade, as if the assignments were trading cards. Jesse had said no, and then regretted saying no, because the Gulf Stream was the one everybody thought they already understood, which meant everybody would notice when he got it wrong.

He had gotten it wrong once already. In November, on the class trip to the science museum, he'd stood in front of the wall-sized current map with Lucille and traced a line straight from Africa to Norway, confident, unhurried. A docent had been standing near the diorama of a research vessel, and Lucille had called her over just to watch Jesse be corrected. The docent hadn't vilified him, though Lucille clearly half-hoped she would. She had just put her own finger on the map at the Gulf of Mexico, drawn it through the narrow strait beside Florida, and run it north along the coast before letting it swing east. "It's called the Gulf Stream," she'd said, and walked away, leaving the whole correction as an accusation Jesse had to decode himself.

Tonight the house was too quiet to think in. His grandfather was in the front room with the radio on, some phone-in program about council spending that seemed designed as background noise rather than content. Jesse carried the map in there and spread it across the ottoman. "I have to explain this tomorrow," he said. "To a class. For a grade."

His grandfather leaned forward, hands on his knees, and looked at the map for a long time. "Which bit's yours?"

"The warm one. The red ribbon that goes up the coast."

His grandfather put a finger at the bottom of the red ribbon, in the bulge of the Gulf of Mexico, and traced it slowly out through the gap between Florida and Cuba, then north, hugging the shoreline, past the Carolinas before it peeled away. He didn't say anything while he did it. He'd been a merchant sailor for thirty years, Jesse remembered, and had probably crossed the thing twice a year without once needing to name it. The gesture itself was a kind of argument: that the current was a fact of the body before it was a fact of the tongue.

Jesse spread the map flat again and got out his phone to time himself. The problem, he decided, was not the route. He could trace the route now with his eyes shut. The problem was the leap at the end, from the ribbon leaving the American coast to the mild winters in Britain, and he had two stories about that leap and no way to choose between them. In one story, the current was an engine, personally responsible, carrying heat like a delivery van. In the other, it was only one line in a larger pattern, a leitmotif rather than the whole melody. Mr. Reddy would ask which was true. Jesse suspected the honest answer was that nobody in the room, including Mr. Reddy, could say precisely where the responsibility began and ended, and that the four minutes would be spent dressing that uncertainty up as confidence.

He tried the explanation out loud anyway, his grandfather as the audience, the radio muttering underneath. "It flows out of the Gulf of Mexico, through the Florida Straits, then north along the east coast of the United States," Jesse said, tracing it, "and the same warm water ends up moderating northern Europe. That part's certain." His grandfather nodded at the right moments. When Jesse stumbled on whether to call the European effect direct or indirect, his grandfather said only, "Say what you know. Leave the rest."

"Mr. Reddy doesn't grade what I leave out."

"He grades whether you sound like you're lying." That was extrinsic to the map, but it was the most useful thing anyone had said to him all week, and Jesse wrote it on his hand in ballpoint.

He practiced until midnight, four minutes and eleven seconds, then three fifty-two, then four minutes exactly, twice. His grandfather fell asleep in the chair somewhere around the third run-through, chin down, the radio still going. Jesse folded the map, set the alarm, and slept on the sofa with his shoes on.

At seven the phone buzzed. Lucille, all capitals: SCHOOL CLOSED. ROADS. REDDY SAYS PRESENTATIONS WHEN WE'RE BACK. Jesse stood at the front window with the map under his arm, dressed, rehearsed, ready, and watched the snow come down over his grandfather's street, thick and unhurried, burying the parked cars to their wheel arches.
